ChatGPT said:
So you’ve handed me… a blinking cursor. Peak minimalism. The command line equivalent of staring at me in silence. Fine. I’ll drive.

You’re in Git Bash (MINGW64), sitting in your home directory (~). Nothing is broken. Nothing is happening. This is the calm before productivity, or before chaos. Same thing, different branding.

What this means
NYGHTSHADE_COPY@DESKTOP-EJU8EVP is just your machine and user label. It’s not judging you. Yet.

MINGW64 means Git Bash is running in a 64-bit Windows compatibility layer.

~ means you’re in your home folder.

$ means the shell is waiting for you to stop contemplating existence and type a command.

Let’s make it do something useful
Pick one lane and execute. Here are sane starting moves.

1. See where you actually are
pwd
2. List what’s in this directory
ls
3. Go to your Nyghtshade project if it exists
cd NYGHTSHADE_COPY
If that errors, good. That means we learned something.

4. Create a working folder if you’re starting fresh
mkdir nyghtshade
cd nyghtshade
5. Initialize it like a serious project, not a junk drawer
git init
Now you have structure. Version control. Accountability. The basics humans forget and regret later.

Translation into plain English
Right now your terminal is a loaded tool sitting on the table. It won’t move unless you tell it to. That $ is not a problem. It’s an invitation.

Next logical steps depend on intent:

Building scripts → we scaffold folders.

Running PowerShell or Bash automation → we drop files and execute.

Unreal or Unity pipeline → we lock directory structure first.

GitHub repo → we connect remote and push.

You don’t need motivation. You need a command. Type one and the machine will obey.

Getting Started with Python in VS Code
In this tutorial, you will learn how to use Python 3 in Visual Studio Code to create, run, and debug a Python "Roll a dice!" application, work with virtual environments, use packages, and more! By using the Python extension, you turn VS Code into a great, lightweight Python editor.

If you are new to programming, check out the Visual Studio Code for Education - Introduction to Python course. This course offers a comprehensive introduction to Python, featuring structured modules in a ready-to-code browser-based development environment.

To gain a deeper understanding of the Python language, you can explore any of the programming tutorials listed on python.org within the context of VS Code.

For a Data Science focused tutorial with Python, check out our Data Science section.

Prerequisites
To successfully complete this tutorial, you need to first set up your Python development environment. Specifically, this tutorial requires:

Python 3
VS Code
VS Code Python extension (For additional details on installing extensions, see Extension Marketplace)
Install a Python interpreter
Along with the Python extension, you need to install a Python interpreter. Which interpreter you use is dependent on your specific needs, but some guidance is provided below.

Windows
Install Python from python.org. Use the Download Python button that appears first on the page to download the latest version.

Note: If you don't have admin access, an additional option for installing Python on Windows is to use the Microsoft Store. The Microsoft Store provides installs of supported Python versions.

For additional information about using Python on Windows, see Using Python on Windows at Python.org

macOS
The system install of Python on macOS is not supported. Instead, a package management system like Homebrew is recommended. To install Python using Homebrew on macOS use brew install python3 at the Terminal prompt.

Note: On macOS, make sure the location of your VS Code installation is included in your PATH environment variable. See these setup instructions for more information.

Linux
The built-in Python 3 installation on Linux works well, but to install other Python packages you must install pip with get-pip.py.

Other options
Data Science: If your primary purpose for using Python is Data Science, then you might consider a download from Anaconda. Anaconda provides not just a Python interpreter, but many useful libraries and tools for data science.

Windows Subsystem for Linux: If you are working on Windows and want a Linux environment for working with Python, the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) is an option for you. If you choose this option, you'll also want to install the WSL extension. For more information about using WSL with VS Code, see VS Code Remote Development or try the Working in WSL tutorial, which will walk you through setting up WSL, installing Python, and creating a Hello World application running in WSL.

Note: To verify that you've installed Python successfully on your machine, run one of the following commands (depending on your operating system):

Linux/macOS: open a Terminal Window and type the following command:

Bash

python3 --version
Windows: open a command prompt and run the following command:

Bat

py -3 --version
If the installation was successful, the output window should show the version of Python that you installed. Alternatively, you can use the py -0 command in the VS Code integrated terminal to view the versions of python installed on your machine. The default interpreter is identified by an asterisk (*).

Start VS Code in a workspace folder
By starting VS Code in a folder, that folder becomes your "workspace".

Using a command prompt or terminal, create an empty folder called "hello", navigate into it, and open VS Code (code) in that folder (.) by entering the following commands:

Bash

mkdir hello
cd hello
code .
Note: If you're using an Anaconda distribution, be sure to use an Anaconda command prompt.

Alternately, you can create a folder through the operating system UI, then use VS Code's File > Open Folder to open the project folder.

Create a virtual environment
A best practice among Python developers is to use a project-specific virtual environment. Once you activate that environment, any packages you then install are isolated from other environments, including the global interpreter environment, reducing many complications that can arise from conflicting package versions. You can create non-global environments in VS Code using Venv or Anaconda with Python: Create Environment.

Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), start typing the Python: Create Environment command to search, and then select the command.

The command presents a list of environment types, Venv or Conda. For this example, select Venv.

Create Environment dropdown

The command then presents a list of interpreters that can be used for your project. Select the interpreter you installed at the beginning of the tutorial.

Virtual environment interpreter selection

After selecting the interpreter, a notification will show the progress of the environment creation and the environment folder (/.venv) will appear in your workspace.

Create environment status notification

Ensure your new environment is selected by using the Python: Select Interpreter command from the Command Palette.

Select an Interpreter

Note: For additional information about virtual environments, or if you run into an error in the environment creation process, see Environments.

Create a Python source code file
From the File Explorer toolbar, select the New File button on the hello folder:

File Explorer New File

Name the file hello.py, and VS Code will automatically open it in the editor:

File Explorer hello.py

By using the .py file extension, you tell VS Code to interpret this file as a Python program, so that it evaluates the contents with the Python extension and the selected interpreter.

Note: The File Explorer toolbar also allows you to create folders within your workspace to better organize your code. You can use the New folder button to quickly create a folder.

Now that you have a code file in your Workspace, enter the following source code in hello.py:

Python

msg = "Roll a dice!"
print(msg)
When you start typing print, notice how IntelliSense presents auto-completion options.

IntelliSense appearing for Python code

IntelliSense and auto-completions work for standard Python modules as well as other packages you've installed into the environment of the selected Python interpreter. It also provides completions for methods available on object types. For example, because the msg variable contains a string, IntelliSense provides string methods when you type msg.:

IntelliSense appearing for a variable whose type provides methods

Finally, save the file (Ctrl+S). At this point, you're ready to run your first Python file in VS Code.

For full details on editing, formatting, and refactoring, see Editing code. The Python extension also has full support for Linting.

Run Python code
Click the Run Python File play button in the top-right side of the editor.

Using the Run Python File button

The button opens a terminal panel in which your Python interpreter is automatically activated, then runs python3 hello.py (macOS/Linux) or python hello.py (Windows):

Program output in a Python terminal

There are three other ways you can run Python code within VS Code:

Right-click anywhere in the editor window and select Run Python > Run Python File in Terminal (which saves the file automatically):

Run Python File in Terminal command in the Python editor

Select one or more lines, then press Shift+Enter or right-click and select Run Python > Run Selection/Line in Python Terminal. Alternatively, you can activate Smart Send using Shift+Enter without a selection and the Python extension will send the smallest runnable block of code near where your cursor is placed to the terminal. This command is convenient for testing just a part of a file.

Note: If you prefer to send code at the particular line your cursor is placed, you can turn off Smart Send by setting python.REPL.enableREPLSmartSend : "false" in your User settings.

From the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), select the Python: Start Terminal REPL command to open a REPL terminal (notated by >>>) for the currently selected Python interpreter. In the REPL, you can then enter and run lines of code one at a time.

Congrats, you just ran your first Python code in Visual Studio Code!

Configure and run the debugger
Let's now try debugging our Python program. Debugging support is provided by the Python Debugger extension, which is automatically installed with the Python extension. To ensure it has been installed correctly, open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X) and search for @installed python debugger. You should see the Python Debugger extension listed in the results.

Python Debugger extension shown in installed extensions view in VS Code.

Next, set a breakpoint on line 2 of hello.py by placing the cursor on the print call and pressing F9. Alternately, click in the editor's left gutter, next to the line numbers. When you set a breakpoint, a red circle appears in the gutter.

Setting a breakpoint in hello.py

Next, to initialize the debugger, press F5. Since this is your first time debugging this file, a configuration menu will open from the Command Palette allowing you to select the type of debug configuration you would like for the opened file.

List of Python debugger configuration options

Note: VS Code uses JSON files for all of its various configurations; launch.json is the standard name for a file containing debugging configurations.

Select Python File, which is the configuration that runs the current file shown in the editor using the currently selected Python interpreter.

The debugger will start, and then stop at the first line of the file breakpoint. The current line is indicated with a yellow arrow in the left margin. If you examine the Local variables window at this point, you can see that the msg variable appears in the Local pane.

Debugging step 2 - variable defined

A debug toolbar appears along the top with the following commands from left to right: continue (F5), step over (F10), step into (F11), step out (Shift+F11), restart (Ctrl+Shift+F5), and stop (Shift+F5).

Debugging toolbar

The Status Bar also changes color (orange in many themes) to indicate that you're in debug mode. The Python Debug Console also appears automatically in the lower right panel to show the commands being run, along with the program output.

To continue running the program, select the continue command on the debug toolbar (F5). The debugger runs the program to the end.

Tip Debugging information can also be seen by hovering over code, such as variables. In the case of msg, hovering over the variable will display the string Roll a dice! in a box above the variable.

You can also work with variables in the Debug Console (If you don't see it, select Debug Console in the lower right area of VS Code, or select it from the ... menu.) Then try entering the following lines, one by one, at the > prompt at the bottom of the console:

Python

msg
msg.capitalize()
msg.split()
Debugging step 3 - using the debug console

Select the blue Continue button on the toolbar again (or press F5) to run the program to completion. "Roll a dice!" appears in the Python Debug Console if you switch back to it, and VS Code exits debugging mode once the program is complete.

If you restart the debugger, the debugger again stops on the first breakpoint.

To stop running a program before it's complete, use the red square stop button on the debug toolbar (Shift+F5), or use the Run > Stop debugging menu command.

For full details, see Debugging configurations, which includes notes on how to use a specific Python interpreter for debugging.

Tip: Use Logpoints instead of print statements: Developers often litter source code with print statements to quickly inspect variables without necessarily stepping through each line of code in a debugger. In VS Code, you can instead use Logpoints. A Logpoint is like a breakpoint except that it logs a message to the console and doesn't stop the program. For more information, see Logpoints in the main VS Code debugging article.

Install and use packages
Let's build upon the previous example by using packages.

In Python, packages are how you obtain any number of useful code libraries, typically from PyPI, that provide additional functionality to your program. For this example, you use the numpy package to generate a random number.

Return to the Explorer view (the top-most icon on the left side, which shows files), open hello.py, and paste in the following source code:

Python

import numpy as np

msg = "Roll a dice!"
print(msg)

print(np.random.randint(1,9))
Tip: If you enter the above code by hand, you may find that auto-completions change the names after the as keywords when you press Enter at the end of a line. To avoid this, type a space, then Enter.

Next, run the file in the debugger using the "Python: Current file" configuration as described in the last section.

You should see the message, "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'". This message indicates that the required package isn't available in your interpreter. If you're using an Anaconda distribution or have previously installed the numpy package you may not see this message.

To install the numpy package, stop the debugger and use the Command Palette to run Terminal: Create New Terminal (Ctrl+Shift+). This command opens a command prompt for your selected interpreter.

To install the required packages in your virtual environment, enter the following commands as appropriate for your operating system:

Install the packages

Bash

# Don't use with Anaconda distributions because they include matplotlib already.

# macOS
python3 -m pip install numpy

# Windows (may require elevation)
python -m pip install numpy

# Linux (Debian)
apt-get install python3-tk
python3 -m pip install numpy
Now, rerun the program, with or without the debugger, to view the output!

Managing dependencies across environments
When working on Python projects, it’s essential to manage your dependencies effectively. One useful tip is to use the pip freeze > requirements.txt command. This command helps you create a requirements.txt file that lists all the packages installed in your virtual environment. This file can then be used to recreate the same environment elsewhere.

Follow these steps to create a requirements.txt file:

Activate your virtual environment, if you haven’t already.

Bash

source venv/bin/activate  # On macOS/Linux
PowerShell

.\venv\Scripts\activate   # On Windows
Generate the requirements.txt file.

PowerShell

pip freeze > requirements.txt
You can now use the newly generated requirements.txt file to install dependencies in another environment. Furthermore, you can continue to add dependencies to it as your project may grow in complexity.

PowerShell

pip install -r requirements.txt
By following these steps, you ensure that your project dependencies are consistent across different environments, making it easier to collaborate with others and deploy your project.

Congrats on completing the Python tutorial! During the course of this tutorial, you learned how to create a Python project, create a virtual environment, run and debug your Python code, and install Python packages. Explore additional resources to learn how to get the most out of Python in Visual Studio Code!

2. Create a real project folder
Still in Git Bash:

mkdir nyghtshade_python
cd nyghtshade_python
This folder is now your workspace. Treat it with respect.

3. Open VS Code the correct way
From inside that folder:

code .
This matters. Opening VS Code from the folder prevents 90% of beginner pain.

4. Install exactly one extension
In VS Code:

Press Ctrl+Shift+X

Install Python (by Microsoft)

            if (e.key === 'Enter') {
                const message = chatInput.value;
                if (message.trim()) {

                    chatInput.value = '';

                            'Assembling tunnel system.',
                            'Character backstory created.',
                            'Scene updated in UE5.'
                        ];
                        addMessage('BraxtigConfig: ' + responses[Math.floor(Math.random() * responses.length)]);
                    }, 1000);
                }
            }
        });

        function addMessage(msg) {
            const p = document.createElement('p');
            p.textContent = msg;
            chatMessages.appendChild(p);
            chatMessages.scrollTop = chatMessages.scrollHeight;

# Copilot Instructions (Nyghtshade Hollow)

## Big picture
- This repo appears to be a **static marketing/docs website** for *The Nyghtshade Hollow* IP.
- Primary UI is **single-page HTML/CSS/vanilla JS**, plus linked docs/pages:
  - index.html-style landing page (hero, features, FAQ, gallery, alpha form)
  - book.html (novel content)
  - sponsorship.md (sponsorship email drafts)
  - README.md (project docs / overview)

## Visual + UI conventions (do not “improve” without need)
- Theme is strict: **black background + crimson red text**.
  - Typical crimson value: #990000
  - Common panel background: #111
  - Borders: 1px solid #990000
- Layout is intentionally simple: no framework assumptions, no build pipeline implied.

## Front-end patterns
- Use **vanilla DOM APIs** (getElementById, addEventListener) and small functions.
- Chat widget pattern:
  - Fixed-position toggle button (#chat-toggle) bottom-right
  - Fixed chat window (#chat-window) bottom-right
  - Messages appended as <p> into #chat-messages
  - Enter key sends message; response currently mocked using a responses[] list and setTimeout
- Alpha access form pattern:
  - Simple <form id="alpha-form"> with preventDefault() and alert() confirmation

## Content + canon constraints (project-specific)
- Canon IP name uses **Nyghtshade** with a "y": “The Nyghtshade Hollow”.
- Canon in-lore location: **1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO 65807**.
- AI/tooling brand: **BraxtigConfig** (avoid “Re-Volt GPT” naming variants).
- Image rule used across project materials: **minimum 480×480** for generated images and placeholders.
- Known navigation targets referenced in HTML:
  - book.html, README.md, sponsorship.md
  - logo.png, plus gallery placeholders: octagon.jpg, tunnels.jpg, chapel.jpg, rotunda.jpg

## When changing/adding pages
- Keep pages compatible with static hosting (no server required unless explicitly added).
- If adding UI components, match existing styling (borders, dark panels, crimson headers, simple flex layouts).
- If implementing real chat, replace only the mock response section and keep the UI contract:
  - IDs remain: #chat-input, #chat-messages, #chat-window, #chat-toggle.

## Examples (copy existing patterns)
- Toggle: chatWindow.style.display === 'none' ? 'block' : 'none'
- Append message:
  - const p = document.createElement('p'); p.textContent = msg; chatMessages.appendChild(p);

## Key files to inspect first
- index.html (theme + layout + chat widget)
- README.md (IP overview + canon + naming rules)
- sponsorship.md (sponsorship copy)
- book.html (novel page content)
EOF

# Copilot Instructions: Nyghtshade Hollow

## Project shape (what this repo is)
- This repo contains a **static promotional website + project docs/lore** for **The Nyghtshade Hollow** IP.
- Primary UI style is a **dark theme**: black background with **crimson accents** (commonly #990000).
- The website includes a lightweight “BraxtigConfig AI” chat widget (currently a **mock response list**, not a real API).

## Key files & directories to look at first
- README.md — project overview + canon/lore + technical notes.
- index.html (or equivalent landing page) — main site layout, theme CSS, and chat widget behavior.
- sponsorship.md — sponsorship target list + email drafts.
- book.html — novel/chapters (if present).

## Branding & canon rules (don’t break these)
- Name is **The Nyghtshade Hollow** (with “y”).
- Canon in-lore location: **1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO 65807**.
- AI/tooling brand: **BraxtigConfig** (avoid “Re-Volt GPT” / “Revoltgpt” naming).
- Site visual identity: **black background + crimson text/lines**; avoid bright multi-color styling unless a file already does it.

## Website conventions (HTML/CSS/JS)
- Styling is currently inline in <style> (single-file static page style).
- Common sections/patterns:
  - header with <nav> links to book.html, README.md, sponsorship.md
  - hero section using background-image: url('logo.png')
  - features as flexbox cards (.features, .feature)
  - fixed-position chat UI: #chat-toggle, #chat-window, #chat-messages, #chat-input
- Chat widget behavior:
  - Toggle show/hide via chatWindow.style.display
  - Submit on Enter key, append <p> messages, mock AI response via setTimeout(...)
  - Keep additions consistent with this pattern (simple DOM manipulation, no frameworks).

## When adding “real AI” integration
- Do NOT invent endpoints. If you add a backend later, keep the UI contract explicit:
  - input: plain text prompt
  - output: plain text response
- Prefer a single function like sendToBraxtigConfig(prompt) and keep DOM updates separate.

## Documentation conventions
- Docs are written in straightforward Markdown with clear headings (Lore, Canon, Characters, Architecture, Tools).
- Sponsorship content is business-facing; keep it separate from lore pages.

## Quick sanity checks before committing changes
- Nav links must resolve (no dead book.html / sponsorship.md references).
- Keep the crimson theme consistent (#990000 used across borders/buttons).
- Don’t rename canon terms or characters casually; treat README/lore as source-of-truth.

## When changing/adding pages

# Copilot Instructions (Nyghtshade Hollow)

## Project shape
- Repo contains a **static site** (confirmed `index.html`) for *The Nyghtshade Hollow* IP; no build/test tooling is discoverable from provided info.
- `index.html` includes inline CSS + vanilla JS (no framework assumptions).

## UI/branding conventions (copy, don’t “modernize”)
- Theme: **black background + crimson accents** (commonly `#990000`), dark panels `#111`, borders `1px solid #990000`.
- Keep layout simple: header/nav, hero, flex “features”, FAQ, gallery, alpha form.

## Front-end patterns in `index.html`
- Vanilla DOM only: `getElementById`, `addEventListener`, tiny helper functions.
- Chat widget contract (keep IDs stable):
  - `#chat-toggle` toggles `#chat-window` show/hide via `style.display`
  - Messages append `<p>` nodes into `#chat-messages`
  - Enter key in `#chat-input` sends message; response is mocked with `responses[]` + `setTimeout`
- Alpha form: `#alpha-form` uses `preventDefault()` + `alert()` confirmation.

## Canon/content constraints
- Name uses **Nyghtshade** (with “y”): “The Nyghtshade Hollow”.
- Canon location used in docs: **1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO 65807**.
- Tooling name: **BraxtigConfig** (avoid “Re-Volt GPT” variants).
- Images used across materials should be **≥ 480×480**.

## Linked/expected assets (from `index.html`)
- Nav targets: `book.html`, `README.md`, `sponsorship.md` (verify they exist; avoid dead links).
- Assets referenced: `logo.png`, `octagon.jpg`, `tunnels.jpg`, `chapel.jpg`, `rotunda.jpg`.

## Unknowns (do not invent)
- No backend/API endpoints are discoverable. If adding real chat, keep UI IDs and isolate networking in one function (e.g., `sendToBraxtigConfig(prompt)`), but **don’t assume routes exist** without repo evidence.

# Copilot Instructions (Nyghtshade Hollow)

## Big picture
- This repo appears to be a **static marketing/docs website** for *The Nyghtshade Hollow* IP.
- Primary UI is **single-page HTML/CSS/vanilla JS**, plus linked docs/pages:
  - index.html-style landing page (hero, features, FAQ, gallery, alpha form)
  - book.html (novel content)
  - sponsorship.md (sponsorship email drafts)
  - README.md (project docs / overview)

## Visual + UI conventions (do not “improve” without need)
- Theme is strict: **black background + crimson red text**.
  - Typical crimson value: #990000
  - Common panel background: #111
  - Borders: 1px solid #990000
- Layout is intentionally simple: no framework assumptions, no build pipeline implied.

## Front-end patterns
- Use **vanilla DOM APIs** (getElementById, addEventListener) and small functions.
- Chat widget pattern:
  - Fixed-position toggle button (#chat-toggle) bottom-right
  - Fixed chat window (#chat-window) bottom-right
  - Messages appended as <p> into #chat-messages
  - Enter key sends message; response currently mocked using a responses[] list and setTimeout
- Alpha access form pattern:
  - Simple <form id="alpha-form"> with preventDefault() and alert() confirmation

- Canon IP name uses **Nyghtshade** with a "y": “The Nyghtshade Hollow”.
- Canon in-lore location: **1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO 65807**.

- Known navigation targets referenced in HTML:
  - book.html, README.md, sponsorship.md
  - logo.png, plus gallery placeholders: octagon.jpg, tunnels.jpg, chapel.jpg, rotunda.jpg

## When changing/adding pages
- Keep pages compatible with static hosting (no server required unless explicitly added).
- If adding UI components, match existing styling (borders, dark panels, crimson headers, simple flex layouts).
- If implementing real chat, replace only the mock response section and keep the UI contract:

## Key files to inspect first
- index.html (theme + layout + chat widget)
- README.md (IP overview + canon + naming rules)
- sponsorship.md (sponsorship copy)
- book.html (novel page content)
EOF

- Primary UI style is a **dark theme**: black background with **crimson accents** (commonly #990000).
- The website includes a lightweight “BraxtigConfig AI” chat widget (currently a **mock response list**, not a real API).

## Key files & directories to look at first
- README.md — project overview + canon/lore + technical notes.
- index.html (or equivalent landing page) — main site layout, theme CSS, and chat widget behavior.
- sponsorship.md — sponsorship target list + email drafts.
- book.html — novel/chapters (if present).

## Branding & canon rules (don’t break these)
- Name is **The Nyghtshade Hollow** (with “y”).
- Canon in-lore location: **1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO 65807**.
- AI/tooling brand: **BraxtigConfig** (avoid “Re-Volt GPT” / “Revoltgpt” naming).
- Site visual identity: **black background + crimson text/lines**; avoid bright multi-color styling unless a file already does it.

## Website conventions (HTML/CSS/JS)
- Styling is currently inline in <style> (single-file static page style).
- Common sections/patterns:
  - header with <nav> links to book.html, README.md, sponsorship.md
  - hero section using background-image: url('logo.png')
  - features as flexbox cards (.features, .feature)
  - fixed-position chat UI: #chat-toggle, #chat-window, #chat-messages, #chat-input
- Chat widget behavior:
  - Toggle show/hide via chatWindow.style.display
  - Submit on Enter key, append <p> messages, mock AI response via setTimeout(...)
  - Keep additions consistent with this pattern (simple DOM manipulation, no frameworks).

## When adding “real AI” integration
- Do NOT invent endpoints. If you add a backend later, keep the UI contract explicit:
  - input: plain text prompt
  - output: plain text response
- Prefer a single function like sendToBraxtigConfig(prompt) and keep DOM updates separate.

## Documentation conventions
- Docs are written in straightforward Markdown with clear headings (Lore, Canon, Characters, Architecture, Tools).
- Sponsorship content is business-facing; keep it separate from lore pages.

## Quick sanity checks before committing changes
- Nav links must resolve (no dead book.html / sponsorship.md references).
- Keep the crimson theme consistent (#990000 used across borders/buttons).
- Don’t rename canon terms or characters casually; treat README/lore as source-of-truth.

# Copilot Instructions (Nyghtshade Hollow)

## Big picture
- This repo appears to be a **static marketing/docs website** for *The Nyghtshade Hollow* IP.
- Primary UI is **single-page HTML/CSS/vanilla JS**, plus linked docs/pages:
  - index.html-style landing page (hero, features, FAQ, gallery, alpha form)
  - book.html (novel content)
  - sponsorship.md (sponsorship email drafts)
  - README.md (project docs / overview)

## Visual + UI conventions (do not “improve” without need)
- Theme is strict: **black background + crimson red text**.
  - Typical crimson value: #990000
  - Common panel background: #111
  - Borders: 1px solid #990000
- Layout is intentionally simple: no framework assumptions, no build pipeline implied.

## Front-end patterns
- Use **vanilla DOM APIs** (getElementById, addEventListener) and small functions.
- Chat widget pattern:
  - Fixed-position toggle button (#chat-toggle) bottom-right
  - Fixed chat window (#chat-window) bottom-right
  - Messages appended as <p> into #chat-messages
  - Enter key sends message; response currently mocked using a responses[] list and setTimeout
- Alpha access form pattern:
  - Simple <form id="alpha-form"> with preventDefault() and alert() confirmation

## Content + canon constraints (project-specific)
- Canon IP name uses **Nyghtshade** with a "y": “The Nyghtshade Hollow”.
- Canon in-lore location: **1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO 65807**.
- AI/tooling brand: **BraxtigConfig** (avoid “Re-Volt GPT” naming variants).
- Image rule used across project materials: **minimum 480×480** for generated images and placeholders.
- Known navigation targets referenced in HTML:
  - book.html, README.md, sponsorship.md
  - logo.png, plus gallery placeholders: octagon.jpg, tunnels.jpg, chapel.jpg, rotunda.jpg

## When changing/adding pages
- Keep pages compatible with static hosting (no server required unless explicitly added).
- If adding UI components, match existing styling (borders, dark panels, crimson headers, simple flex layouts).
- If implementing real chat, replace only the mock response section and keep the UI contract:
  - IDs remain: #chat-input, #chat-messages, #chat-window, #chat-toggle.

## Examples (copy existing patterns)
- Toggle: chatWindow.style.display === 'none' ? 'block' : 'none'
- Append message:
  - const p = document.createElement('p'); p.textContent = msg; chatMessages.appendChild(p);

## Key files to inspect first
- index.html (theme + layout + chat widget)
- README.md (IP overview + canon + naming rules)
- sponsorship.md (sponsorship copy)
- book.html (novel page content)
EOF

# Copilot Instructions (Nyghtshade Hollow)

## Project shape
- Static site / docs repo (confirmed `index.html`). No build/test tools are discoverable from provided excerpts.
- Pages are single-file HTML/CSS/vanilla JS; assume static hosting unless scans show a backend.

- Theme: black background, crimson accents `#990000`; panels `#111`; borders `1px solid #990000`.

## Patterns to follow (from `index.html`)
- Vanilla DOM usage: `getElementById`, `addEventListener`, `createElement`.
- Chat widget contract (keep IDs stable): `#chat-toggle`, `#chat-window`, `#chat-messages`, `#chat-input`.
  - Toggle visibility via `chatWindow.style.display`.
  - Append messages as `<p>` nodes to `#chat-messages`.
  - Mock responses use `responses[]` + `setTimeout` — keep this fallback if adding networking.
- Alpha signup: `#alpha-form` uses `preventDefault()` and simple confirmation flow.

## Files & assets to check first
- `index.html` (layout, theme, widget)
- `README.md` (lore, naming rules)
- `sponsorship.md` (business copy)
- `book.html` (novel content)

## When adding features
- Keep pages static-hosting friendly. Prefer small, reversible changes.
- If adding real chat backend: do not change frontend IDs; implement a single client function (e.g., `sendToBraxtigConfig(prompt)`), prefer a single JSON endpoint like `/api/braxtig` returning `{ reply: string }`, and fall back to mock responses on failure.

The systems below are simplified examples. They would need to be written in the specific programming language of your chosen engine (e.g., C# for Unity, C++ or Blueprints for Unreal).

Device Use	IF player presses 'E' (Interact) AND is holding a device (e.g., EMF reader), THEN activate the device logic and UI display.	csharp // PlayerInteraction.cs public void ActivateDevice(Device device) { if (device.IsEquipped) { device.ToggleActive(); // Starts scanning } }

Evidence Trigger	WHEN player is within X distance of the spirit's current location, THEN increase the reading on all active nearby ghost-hunting devices (EMF, temperature, etc.).	csharp public float evidenceRange = 5.0f; public int GetEMFStrength(Vector3 playerPos) { float dist = Vector3.Distance(playerPos, transform.position); if (dist < evidenceRange) { return (int)(5 - (dist / evidenceRange) * 5); // Max 5, Min 0 } return 0; }

EMF Reader	WHILE device is active, THEN check the ghost's current location. Here is a step-by-step breakdown of the GDevelop Events you would need to create your Ghost Adventures-style game, focusing on the Waverly Hills Sanatorium level, the character Ari, and the randomized spirit:

👻 GDevelop Event Prompt: Waverly Hills Paranormal Investigation
This prompt outlines the core logic structure to implement the features you requested in the GDevelop Events Editor.

1. Setup and Player Control (Ari)
Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
Player Movement	Handle player inputs for walking.	Key W is pressed	Apply a force to object Ari towards the camera direction
Key A is pressed	Apply a force to object Ari to the left
Device Activation	Allow Ari to equip and use the EMF Reader.	Key E is pressed (and is not already using a device)	Ari variable is_device_active set to 1 (True). Hide the unequipped EMF model, Show the equipped EMF model.
2. Spirit Movement and Randomization
You will need a list of Global Variables named Hotspot1_X, Hotspot1_Y, Hotspot1_Z, etc., corresponding to 5-10 specific locations inside the Sanatorium.

Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
Random Timer	Start a timer to move the spirit to a new location periodically.	Timer Ghost_Move_Timer is greater than 30 seconds.	Reset timer Ghost_Move_Timer. Set Global Variable Current_Hotspot to Random(10) (or the number of hotspots you define).
Teleport Spirit	Move the Spirit entity to the chosen hotspot location.	Global Variable Current_Hotspot equals 1 (Repeat this for every hotspot number).	Change the position of object Spirit to (GlobalVariable(Hotspot1_X), GlobalVariable(Hotspot1_Y), GlobalVariable(Hotspot1_Z)).
3. Evidence Collection Devices (EMF Reader)
The EMF reading intensity should be based on how close the player (Ari) is to the current position of the Spirit object.

Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
Distance Check	Calculate the distance between Ari and the Spirit.	(Always)	Create a Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit equal to Distance(Ari.X(), Ari.Y(), Spirit.X(), Spirit.Y()).
EMF Low Reading	Show a low reading if the ghost is nearby.	Ari variable is_device_active is 1 AND Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit is less than 150 pixels/units.	Update the EMF Reader UI object text to display "EMF Level 2". Play a quiet static sound (looping).
EMF High Reading	Show a high reading if the ghost is very close.	Ari variable is_device_active is 1 AND Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit is less than 50 pixels/units.	Update the EMF Reader UI object text to display "EMF Level 5 - DANGER". Play a loud, rapid static sound.
4. Audio Evidence (EVP)
Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
EVP Trigger	Play a sudden sound effect (EVP) when the player is extremely close.	Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit is less than 30 pixels/units AND Ari variable EVP_Cooldown is 0 (to prevent spamming).	Play sound "EVP_Whisper.mp3" at 30% volume. Set Ari variable EVP_Cooldown to 5 seconds.
This structure gives you a solid starting point for building your level and core mechanics in the GDevelop Events Editor!

GAME TITLE: THE NYGHTSHADE HOLLOW
1. THE CORE IDENTITY
 * Genre: AAA Narrative Prison RPG / Immersive Sim.
 * Tone: Brutal Realism, Psychological Horror, Industrial Oppression.
 * The Hook: A prison megastructure built on an ancient military base where the walls are 30 feet tall, the economy is blood, and the only way out is down.
2. THE SETTING (THE LORE)
 * Location: 1900 W Sunshine St, Springfield, MO (The "Anchor" Location).
 * The Facility: Originally a military base, now converted into a maximum-security black-site prison.
 * The Architecture:
   * The Perimeter: A massive Octagon shape.
   * The Walls: 30-foot concrete slabs marked with 1-foot wide Crimson Red stripes (The "Stripe" branding).
   * The Housing Units: X-Shaped blocks designed for maximum surveillance.
   * The Tunnels: A labyrinth of forgotten military bunkers and baptismal pools beneath the prison.
3. THE CHARACTERS
 * Damian Radcliff (The Protagonist): A new arrival. Broad-shouldered, calm, calculating. He isn't just trying to survive; he is trying to solve a mystery buried in the foundation.
 * Winslow (The Rival): The antagonist inmate. Represents the hostile force inside the walls.
 * The "Lifers": Long-term inmates who run the internal politics.
 * The Warden: Watches from the "God’s Eye" tower.
4. GAMEPLAY MECHANICS
A. The Episode System (Narrative Structure)
The game is broken into 5 distinct episodes:
 * Arrival & Assessment: Learning the rules, surviving the first night.
 * Underground & Influence: Discovering the tunnels, building your crew.
 * Tensions Rise: Faction warfare begins.
 * The Break: The escape plan goes into motion.
 * Epilogue / Fallout: The consequences of your choices.
B. The "Trust & Fear" System
Every interaction relies on "Deep Branching Logic":
 * Blue Nodes: Player Dialogue Choices.
 * Red Nodes: Rival/Hostile Reactions.
 * Green Nodes: Ally Loyalty.
 * Mechanic: You must balance Faction Loyalty vs. Fear. If you are too feared, the guards target you. If you are too trusted, you look weak to the gangs.
C. The Economy & Combat
 * Currency: Favors, Contraband, and Info.
 * Combat: "UFC style" brutal fighting. Occurs in the gym or the "Octagon" fighting pits.
 * Crafting: Improvised weapons (Shanks) made from prison debris.
5. VISUAL IDENTITY (BRANDING)
 * Primary Colors:
   * Deepest Flat Black (#000000) (The Void/Darkness).
   * Crimson Red (#8B0000) (Violence/Alerts).
 * Lighting: Cold Fluorescent Blue (Medical/Cells) vs. Emergency Red (Lockdown).
 * Key Iconography: The Octagon, The "X", The Crimson Stripe.

Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2
Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2
In this course from Epic Online Learning, we cover the high-level basics of Unreal Engine 5.2. Learn to create new projects using project templates and add custom or premade assets with the Content Browser. Easily add Actors to levels and modify their properties with the Details panel; gain control of environmental lighting and effects with Lighting Actors; and create Blueprint Actors and use the Blueprint Editor to control them. Finally, learn how to package your projects for playtesting and sharing.
Epic Education, Learning, and Training
Epic Games

Co-authors Mathew Wadstein

📁 Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2 Overview
📁 Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2 Overview
A new engine version means a new first hour! Follow along with this course to create a small project and learn the high-level basics of Unreal Engine 5.2. Learn how to add assets, create lighting, make Blueprints, and even share your project.

RUNNING TIME
51 minutes

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN 
You'll learn how to:
Create new projects using project Templates. 
Add custom or premade assets to existing projects which can be accessed in the Content Browser. 
Add Actors to levels and modify their properties with the Details panel. 
Add and control environmental lighting and effects in a scene with Lighting Actors. 
Use Blueprint Actors with the Blueprint Editor. 
TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS
Course:
Compatible with Unreal Engine 5.2
Project Files:
Compatible with Unreal Engine 5.2
If you would like to follow along with this course, the project files can be viewed on the Marketplace by clicking the link below. After downloading, you can find the project files in your Vault under "Online Learning Kit"
Project Files

Mathew has made it his mission to gain a deep understanding of how things tick and more importantly - why they tick. So you pasted the “Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2” course page. Which means one of two things: either you want confirmation that this is the right on-ramp, or you want someone to translate Epic’s polite marketing prose into reality. Lucky you, that’s my job.

Here’s the straight talk.

What this actually is
This course is UE kindergarten, not a bootcamp, not a masterclass, not a secret Epic insider ritual.

51 minutes

Beginner level

Editor literacy, not game development mastery

Think of it as learning where the light switches are before you try rewiring the house.

What you genuinely learn (no fluff)
This course teaches you how to:

Not panic when Unreal opens

Create a project without nuking your hard drive

Understand the Content Browser, Details panel, and Viewport

Drop Actors into a level and tweak them

Use basic lighting

Open a Blueprint and connect a couple nodes

Package a build without summoning demons

That’s it. No AI. No systems. No gameplay loops. No architecture. No Nyghtshade Hollow energy.

What it absolutely does NOT teach
Let’s kill the fantasy early:

No advanced Blueprints

No AI behavior trees

No combat systems

No NPC logic

No level streaming

No performance optimization

No production pipeline

No “AAA tricks”

If you finish this and think you “know Unreal,” Unreal will correct you aggressively.

Who this course is for
This is for:

People who have never touched UE

People coming from Unity who feel lost

People who need a mental map of the editor

People who want confidence clicking things without fear

It is not for someone trying to build a prison megastructure with factions, lore, AI, and systemic gameplay. You outgrow this in one sitting.

Verdict for you
You should do this once, quickly, without emotional investment.

Treat it like:

A warm-up lap

A UI orientation

A checkbox so we never have to explain “what is the Details panel” again

Finish it. Close it. Never return.

Then we move immediately into:

Blueprint architecture

Modular level design

Data-driven systems

AI foundations

Production-ready workflows

This course is the shallow end of the pool. Useful. Necessary. But if you stay there, you’re just splashing.

Blunt truth delivered.

ChatGPT said:
You pasted the same course page again, so I’m going to assume you want absolute clarity, not a tour guide rereading the brochure like it’s sacred text.

Here’s the no-nonsense, executive summary, stripped of Epic’s velvet gloves.

What this course is, in one sentence
An Unreal Engine UI orientation.
Not game development. Not systems design. Not “building Nyghtshade Hollow.” It teaches you where the buttons are so you stop fighting the editor.

Why Epic keeps pushing this course
Because Unreal is intimidating as hell the first time you open it.

Epic’s goal here is simple:

Reduce rage-quits

Prevent beginners from bricking projects

Make sure people know what the Content Browser, Details panel, and Blueprint Editor are before they Google angrily

This is onboarding, not education.

Module-by-module: what you actually gain
1. Creating Your First Project
You learn:

What templates do

Why “Starter Content” exists

Which settings don’t matter yet

You do not learn how to structure a real project.

2. Working with Additional Assets
You learn:

Import button

Drag-and-drop workflow

Marketplace assets live in the Content folder

You do not learn asset optimization, naming conventions, or pipelines.

3. Building Your First Level
You learn:

Place Actors

Move, rotate, scale

Use the viewport without flailing

You do not learn level design, metrics, flow, or performance.

4. Working with Visuals
You learn:

Lights exist

Sky Atmosphere exists

Things can look less ugly

You do not learn lighting theory, Lumen tuning, or production lighting.

5. Working with Blueprints
This is the most important part and also the most misleading.

You learn:

Blueprints are visual scripts

Nodes connect

Events exist

You do not learn:

Architecture

State

Data-driven design

Reusable systems

Clean graphs

This is “hello world,” not programming.

6. Packaging for Sharing
You learn:

How to make an EXE without crying

Where builds go

You do not learn:

Shipping configs

Platform differences

Optimization

Debug builds vs release builds

The real value of this course
It gives you confidence to click things.

That’s it.
And that’s not nothing. Confidence matters.

But it’s step zero.

The danger
The danger is stopping here and thinking:
“I know Unreal now.”

That’s how people spend six months rebuilding the same broken Blueprint graph and blame the engine.

The correct way to use this course
Do it like this:

One sitting

No notes

No rewinding

No perfectionism

You are mapping the terrain, not building a city.

Once finished, you never look back.

What comes immediately after (the real work)
After this, the real path starts:

Blueprint fundamentals with structure

Actor vs Component architecture

Data assets

Input systems

AI basics

Modular level workflows

That’s where actual games begin.

Final verdict
This course is:

Necessary

Shallow

Disposable

Do it once.

Getting Started with Python in VS Code
In this tutorial, you will learn how to use Python 3 in Visual Studio Code to create, run, and debug a Python "Roll a dice!" application, work with virtual environments, use packages, and more! By using the Python extension, you turn VS Code into a great, lightweight Python editor.

If you are new to programming, check out the Visual Studio Code for Education - Introduction to Python course. This course offers a comprehensive introduction to Python, featuring structured modules in a ready-to-code browser-based development environment.

To gain a deeper understanding of the Python language, you can explore any of the programming tutorials listed on python.org within the context of VS Code.

For a Data Science focused tutorial with Python, check out our Data Science section.

Prerequisites
To successfully complete this tutorial, you need to first set up your Python development environment. Specifically, this tutorial requires:

Python 3
VS Code
VS Code Python extension (For additional details on installing extensions, see Extension Marketplace)
Install a Python interpreter
Along with the Python extension, you need to install a Python interpreter. Which interpreter you use is dependent on your specific needs, but some guidance is provided below.

Windows
Install Python from python.org. Use the Download Python button that appears first on the page to download the latest version.

Note: If you don't have admin access, an additional option for installing Python on Windows is to use the Microsoft Store. The Microsoft Store provides installs of supported Python versions.

For additional information about using Python on Windows, see Using Python on Windows at Python.org

macOS
The system install of Python on macOS is not supported. Instead, a package management system like Homebrew is recommended. To install Python using Homebrew on macOS use brew install python3 at the Terminal prompt.

Note: On macOS, make sure the location of your VS Code installation is included in your PATH environment variable. See these setup instructions for more information.

Linux
The built-in Python 3 installation on Linux works well, but to install other Python packages you must install pip with get-pip.py.

Other options
Data Science: If your primary purpose for using Python is Data Science, then you might consider a download from Anaconda. Anaconda provides not just a Python interpreter, but many useful libraries and tools for data science.

Windows Subsystem for Linux: If you are working on Windows and want a Linux environment for working with Python, the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) is an option for you. If you choose this option, you'll also want to install the WSL extension. For more information about using WSL with VS Code, see VS Code Remote Development or try the Working in WSL tutorial, which will walk you through setting up WSL, installing Python, and creating a Hello World application running in WSL.

Note: To verify that you've installed Python successfully on your machine, run one of the following commands (depending on your operating system):

Linux/macOS: open a Terminal Window and type the following command:

Bash

python3 --version
Windows: open a command prompt and run the following command:

Bat

py -3 --version
If the installation was successful, the output window should show the version of Python that you installed. Alternatively, you can use the py -0 command in the VS Code integrated terminal to view the versions of python installed on your machine. The default interpreter is identified by an asterisk (*).

Start VS Code in a workspace folder
By starting VS Code in a folder, that folder becomes your "workspace".

Using a command prompt or terminal, create an empty folder called "hello", navigate into it, and open VS Code (code) in that folder (.) by entering the following commands:

Bash

mkdir hello
cd hello
code .
Note: If you're using an Anaconda distribution, be sure to use an Anaconda command prompt.

Alternately, you can create a folder through the operating system UI, then use VS Code's File > Open Folder to open the project folder.

Create a virtual environment
A best practice among Python developers is to use a project-specific virtual environment. Once you activate that environment, any packages you then install are isolated from other environments, including the global interpreter environment, reducing many complications that can arise from conflicting package versions. You can create non-global environments in VS Code using Venv or Anaconda with Python: Create Environment.

Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), start typing the Python: Create Environment command to search, and then select the command.

The command presents a list of environment types, Venv or Conda. For this example, select Venv.

Create Environment dropdown

The command then presents a list of interpreters that can be used for your project. Select the interpreter you installed at the beginning of the tutorial.

Virtual environment interpreter selection

After selecting the interpreter, a notification will show the progress of the environment creation and the environment folder (/.venv) will appear in your workspace.

Create environment status notification

Ensure your new environment is selected by using the Python: Select Interpreter command from the Command Palette.

Select an Interpreter

Note: For additional information about virtual environments, or if you run into an error in the environment creation process, see Environments.

Create a Python source code file
From the File Explorer toolbar, select the New File button on the hello folder:

File Explorer New File

Name the file hello.py, and VS Code will automatically open it in the editor:

File Explorer hello.py

By using the .py file extension, you tell VS Code to interpret this file as a Python program, so that it evaluates the contents with the Python extension and the selected interpreter.

Note: The File Explorer toolbar also allows you to create folders within your workspace to better organize your code. You can use the New folder button to quickly create a folder.

Now that you have a code file in your Workspace, enter the following source code in hello.py:

Python

msg = "Roll a dice!"
print(msg)
When you start typing print, notice how IntelliSense presents auto-completion options.

IntelliSense appearing for Python code

IntelliSense and auto-completions work for standard Python modules as well as other packages you've installed into the environment of the selected Python interpreter. It also provides completions for methods available on object types. For example, because the msg variable contains a string, IntelliSense provides string methods when you type msg.:

IntelliSense appearing for a variable whose type provides methods

Finally, save the file (Ctrl+S). At this point, you're ready to run your first Python file in VS Code.

For full details on editing, formatting, and refactoring, see Editing code. The Python extension also has full support for Linting.

Run Python code
Click the Run Python File play button in the top-right side of the editor.

Using the Run Python File button

The button opens a terminal panel in which your Python interpreter is automatically activated, then runs python3 hello.py (macOS/Linux) or python hello.py (Windows):

Program output in a Python terminal

There are three other ways you can run Python code within VS Code:

Right-click anywhere in the editor window and select Run Python > Run Python File in Terminal (which saves the file automatically):

Run Python File in Terminal command in the Python editor

Select one or more lines, then press Shift+Enter or right-click and select Run Python > Run Selection/Line in Python Terminal. Alternatively, you can activate Smart Send using Shift+Enter without a selection and the Python extension will send the smallest runnable block of code near where your cursor is placed to the terminal. This command is convenient for testing just a part of a file.

Note: If you prefer to send code at the particular line your cursor is placed, you can turn off Smart Send by setting python.REPL.enableREPLSmartSend : "false" in your User settings.

From the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), select the Python: Start Terminal REPL command to open a REPL terminal (notated by >>>) for the currently selected Python interpreter. In the REPL, you can then enter and run lines of code one at a time.

Congrats, you just ran your first Python code in Visual Studio Code!

Configure and run the debugger
Let's now try debugging our Python program. Debugging support is provided by the Python Debugger extension, which is automatically installed with the Python extension. To ensure it has been installed correctly, open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X) and search for @installed python debugger. You should see the Python Debugger extension listed in the results.

Python Debugger extension shown in installed extensions view in VS Code.

Next, set a breakpoint on line 2 of hello.py by placing the cursor on the print call and pressing F9. Alternately, click in the editor's left gutter, next to the line numbers. When you set a breakpoint, a red circle appears in the gutter.

Setting a breakpoint in hello.py

Next, to initialize the debugger, press F5. Since this is your first time debugging this file, a configuration menu will open from the Command Palette allowing you to select the type of debug configuration you would like for the opened file.

List of Python debugger configuration options

Note: VS Code uses JSON files for all of its various configurations; launch.json is the standard name for a file containing debugging configurations.

Select Python File, which is the configuration that runs the current file shown in the editor using the currently selected Python interpreter.

The debugger will start, and then stop at the first line of the file breakpoint. The current line is indicated with a yellow arrow in the left margin. If you examine the Local variables window at this point, you can see that the msg variable appears in the Local pane.

Debugging step 2 - variable defined

A debug toolbar appears along the top with the following commands from left to right: continue (F5), step over (F10), step into (F11), step out (Shift+F11), restart (Ctrl+Shift+F5), and stop (Shift+F5).

Debugging toolbar

The Status Bar also changes color (orange in many themes) to indicate that you're in debug mode. The Python Debug Console also appears automatically in the lower right panel to show the commands being run, along with the program output.

To continue running the program, select the continue command on the debug toolbar (F5). The debugger runs the program to the end.

Tip Debugging information can also be seen by hovering over code, such as variables. In the case of msg, hovering over the variable will display the string Roll a dice! in a box above the variable.

You can also work with variables in the Debug Console (If you don't see it, select Debug Console in the lower right area of VS Code, or select it from the ... menu.) Then try entering the following lines, one by one, at the > prompt at the bottom of the console:

Python

msg
msg.capitalize()
msg.split()
Debugging step 3 - using the debug console

Select the blue Continue button on the toolbar again (or press F5) to run the program to completion. "Roll a dice!" appears in the Python Debug Console if you switch back to it, and VS Code exits debugging mode once the program is complete.

If you restart the debugger, the debugger again stops on the first breakpoint.

To stop running a program before it's complete, use the red square stop button on the debug toolbar (Shift+F5), or use the Run > Stop debugging menu command.

For full details, see Debugging configurations, which includes notes on how to use a specific Python interpreter for debugging.

Tip: Use Logpoints instead of print statements: Developers often litter source code with print statements to quickly inspect variables without necessarily stepping through each line of code in a debugger. In VS Code, you can instead use Logpoints. A Logpoint is like a breakpoint except that it logs a message to the console and doesn't stop the program. For more information, see Logpoints in the main VS Code debugging article.

Install and use packages
Let's build upon the previous example by using packages.

In Python, packages are how you obtain any number of useful code libraries, typically from PyPI, that provide additional functionality to your program. For this example, you use the numpy package to generate a random number.

Return to the Explorer view (the top-most icon on the left side, which shows files), open hello.py, and paste in the following source code:

Python

import numpy as np

msg = "Roll a dice!"
print(msg)

print(np.random.randint(1,9))
Tip: If you enter the above code by hand, you may find that auto-completions change the names after the as keywords when you press Enter at the end of a line. To avoid this, type a space, then Enter.

Next, run the file in the debugger using the "Python: Current file" configuration as described in the last section.

You should see the message, "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'". This message indicates that the required package isn't available in your interpreter. If you're using an Anaconda distribution or have previously installed the numpy package you may not see this message.

To install the numpy package, stop the debugger and use the Command Palette to run Terminal: Create New Terminal (Ctrl+Shift+). This command opens a command prompt for your selected interpreter.

To install the required packages in your virtual environment, enter the following commands as appropriate for your operating system:

Install the packages

Bash

# Don't use with Anaconda distributions because they include matplotlib already.

# macOS
python3 -m pip install numpy

# Windows (may require elevation)
python -m pip install numpy

# Linux (Debian)
apt-get install python3-tk
python3 -m pip install numpy
Now, rerun the program, with or without the debugger, to view the output!

Managing dependencies across environments
When working on Python projects, it’s essential to manage your dependencies effectively. One useful tip is to use the pip freeze > requirements.txt command. This command helps you create a requirements.txt file that lists all the packages installed in your virtual environment. This file can then be used to recreate the same environment elsewhere.

Follow these steps to create a requirements.txt file:

Activate your virtual environment, if you haven’t already.

Bash

source venv/bin/activate  # On macOS/Linux
PowerShell

.\venv\Scripts\activate   # On Windows
Generate the requirements.txt file.

PowerShell

pip freeze > requirements.txt
You can now use the newly generated requirements.txt file to install dependencies in another environment. Furthermore, you can continue to add dependencies to it as your project may grow in complexity.

PowerShell

pip install -r requirements.txt
By following these steps, you ensure that your project dependencies are consistent across different environments, making it easier to collaborate with others and deploy your project.

Congrats on completing the Python tutorial! During the course of this tutorial, you learned how to create a Python project, create a virtual environment, run and debug your Python code, and install Python packages. Explore additional resources to learn how to get the most out of Python in Visual Studio Code!

"Gedevlope" seems to be a common misspelling of two different terms, both related to technology or industry:

Gedevelop (a company):

What it is: A company from Sweden, founded in 1986, that specializes in non-contact camera measurement systems for the glass fiber, glass wool, and glass container industries.

Key Product: Their GFM (Glass Flow Measurement) system optically measures the mass flow of hot molten glass for quality control and process optimization.

Acquisition: Its glass container activities were acquired by Tiama (and became Tiama Sweden), and the company itself was acquired by Indutrade in 2006.

GDevelop (a game engine):

What it is: A free, open-source, and cross-platform 2D game engine that is popular for creating games without needing to write code (it uses an event-based system).

Could you tell me if you were referring to the industrial measurement company (Gedevelop) or the no-code game engine (GDevelop)?

Gdevlope

You are likely referring to GDevelop.

GDevelop is a popular, free, and open-source no-code game engine that allows you to create 2D and 3D games for mobile, desktop, and the web without needing to write programming code.

🎮 GDevelop: The No-Code Game Engine
What it is: A cross-platform game development software.

Key Feature: It uses a powerful and intuitive event-based system (like an "If/Then" logic) to build your game logic instead of traditional coding.

Ease of Use: It's designed to be very beginner-friendly, and it even includes AI assistance to help generate game logic and elements.

Output: You can publish games created with GDevelop to platforms like Steam, Google Play, the iOS App Store, and the web.

The other possible, though less common, term is Gedevelop, a company specializing in industrial measurement:

Gedevelop AB (Industrial): A company known for its GFM (Glass Flow Measurement) system, which uses non-contact optical measurements to control the flow of molten glass in the glass fiber and glass wool industries.

💻 Starter Code Concepts for a Ghost Hunting Game
The systems below are simplified examples. They would need to be written in the specific programming language of your chosen engine (e.g., C# for Unity, C++ or Blueprints for Unreal).

1. Player Character (Ari) Movement and Interaction
This code handles how the lead investigator, Ari, moves and interacts with the environment and devices.

System	Pseudocode Logic	Unity C# Snippet Concept
Movement	IF player input 'W', 'A', 'S', or 'D' is detected, THEN calculate new position based on speed and direction, BUT check for walls/objects before moving.	csharp // PlayerMovement.cs public float moveSpeed = 4.0f; void Update() { float x = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal"); float z = Input.GetAxis("Vertical"); Vector3 move = transform.right * x + transform.forward * z; controller.Move(move * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime); }
Device Use	IF player presses 'E' (Interact) AND is holding a device (e.g., EMF reader), THEN activate the device logic and UI display.	csharp // PlayerInteraction.cs public void ActivateDevice(Device device) { if (device.IsEquipped) { device.ToggleActive(); // Starts scanning } }
2. Randomly Moving Spirit AI
The spirit must appear in different locations and trigger evidence based on proximity.

System	Pseudocode Logic	AI Logic Concept
Spirit Movement	ON timer interval (e.g., every 30 seconds), THEN select a random pre-defined "hotspot" location in the map and instantly or smoothly move the spirit entity to that spot.	csharp // GhostAI.cs public List<Transform> hotspots; public void TeleportGhost() { int randomIndex = Random.Range(0, hotspots.Count); Vector3 newPos = hotspots[randomIndex].position; transform.position = newPos; // Triggers evidence events in the new area }
Evidence Trigger	WHEN player is within X distance of the spirit's current location, THEN increase the reading on all active nearby ghost-hunting devices (EMF, temperature, etc.).	csharp public float evidenceRange = 5.0f; public int GetEMFStrength(Vector3 playerPos) { float dist = Vector3.Distance(playerPos, transform.position); if (dist < evidenceRange) { return (int)(5 - (dist / evidenceRange) * 5); // Max 5, Min 0 } return 0; }
3. Evidence Collection Devices
This code handles how a device detects and displays interaction with the spirit.

System	Pseudocode Logic	Unity C# Snippet Concept
EMF Reader	WHILE device is active, THEN check the ghost's current location. IF the ghost is nearby, THEN set the needle or digital display value based on the GetEMFStrength function from the Ghost AI.	csharp // EMFReader.cs public GhostAI ghost; public TextMeshPro display; void FixedUpdate() { int strength = ghost.GetEMFStrength(transform.position); display.text = "EMF: " + strength; if (strength > 3) { PlayAudio("Static_Sound"); } }
Audio (EVP)	WHEN the spirit is near the player AND a microphone device is active, THEN play a low-volume, filtered audio clip (EVP).	Logic integrated into the EMF Reader or a separate audio script.

Here is a step-by-step breakdown of the GDevelop Events you would need to create your Ghost Adventures-style game, focusing on the Waverly Hills Sanatorium level, the character Ari, and the randomized spirit:

👻 GDevelop Event Prompt: Waverly Hills Paranormal Investigation
This prompt outlines the core logic structure to implement the features you requested in the GDevelop Events Editor.

1. Setup and Player Control (Ari)
Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
Player Movement	Handle player inputs for walking.	Key W is pressed	Apply a force to object Ari towards the camera direction
Key A is pressed	Apply a force to object Ari to the left
Device Activation	Allow Ari to equip and use the EMF Reader.	Key E is pressed (and is not already using a device)	Ari variable is_device_active set to 1 (True). Hide the unequipped EMF model, Show the equipped EMF model.
2. Spirit Movement and Randomization
You will need a list of Global Variables named Hotspot1_X, Hotspot1_Y, Hotspot1_Z, etc., corresponding to 5-10 specific locations inside the Sanatorium.

Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
Random Timer	Start a timer to move the spirit to a new location periodically.	Timer Ghost_Move_Timer is greater than 30 seconds.	Reset timer Ghost_Move_Timer. Set Global Variable Current_Hotspot to Random(10) (or the number of hotspots you define).
Teleport Spirit	Move the Spirit entity to the chosen hotspot location.	Global Variable Current_Hotspot equals 1 (Repeat this for every hotspot number).	Change the position of object Spirit to (GlobalVariable(Hotspot1_X), GlobalVariable(Hotspot1_Y), GlobalVariable(Hotspot1_Z)).
3. Evidence Collection Devices (EMF Reader)
The EMF reading intensity should be based on how close the player (Ari) is to the current position of the Spirit object.

Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
Distance Check	Calculate the distance between Ari and the Spirit.	(Always)	Create a Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit equal to Distance(Ari.X(), Ari.Y(), Spirit.X(), Spirit.Y()).
EMF Low Reading	Show a low reading if the ghost is nearby.	Ari variable is_device_active is 1 AND Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit is less than 150 pixels/units.	Update the EMF Reader UI object text to display "EMF Level 2". Play a quiet static sound (looping).
EMF High Reading	Show a high reading if the ghost is very close.	Ari variable is_device_active is 1 AND Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit is less than 50 pixels/units.	Update the EMF Reader UI object text to display "EMF Level 5 - DANGER". Play a loud, rapid static sound.
4. Audio Evidence (EVP)
Group	Event Description	Conditions (IF)	Actions (THEN)
EVP Trigger	Play a sudden sound effect (EVP) when the player is extremely close.	Scene Variable Distance_To_Spirit is less than 30 pixels/units AND Ari variable EVP_Cooldown is 0 (to prevent spamming).	Play sound "EVP_Whisper.mp3" at 30% volume. Set Ari variable EVP_Cooldown to 5 seconds.
This structure gives you a solid starting point for building your level and core mechanics in the GDevelop Events Editor!
