Generate Code for Nyghtshade Hollow Prison Builder

Nyghtshade Hollow Prison Builder Module – Implementation Plan
Layout System (Dynamic Modular Construction)
The Layout System provides a flexible framework to construct Nyghtshade Hollow’s prison architecture in a modular fashion. It generates the prison’s octagonal overall footprint and populates it with key structural modules like walls, fences, housing units, and connecting corridors, following the established canon design. The goal is to allow designers (or an AI pipeline) to easily reconfigure or regenerate the prison layout while preserving its iconic structure. Key features include:
Octagonal Perimeter & Fences: The entire prison is enclosed by an octagon-shaped outer wall, with triple fence lines following the octagonal shape for layered security. The builder defines an OuterWall module (and corresponding fence modules) that can be placed eight times in an octagonal arrangement. Each wall segment is parameterized (length ~330 ft each side) and the system ensures proper 135° corner angles for a closed octagon. The perimeter wall and fences are generated first as the foundational boundary of the prison.
Central “Spine” and Facility Hubs: A central north-south corridor (the “Spine”) divides the complex and houses administrative and high-security facilities. The builder includes a SpineSegment prefab/Blueprint (BP_SpineSegment) to construct this backbone. It instantiates modules for the Warden’s tower, admin offices, medical ward, security control hub, intake/processing, and visitation areas along this spine. These modules snap together along the central axis (with engine units standardized – 1 Unreal Unit = 1 Unity unit = 1 foot). The spine is placed running through the octagon’s center from north to south, effectively splitting the yard and housing areas as per canon.
Housing Unit Generation: On the west side of the spine, the builder spawns housing units – cellblock structures where inmates live. According to canon, there are 10 multi-story housing units on that side. Each housing unit is built from a Blueprint prefab (BP_HousingUnit) that encapsulates an X-shaped layout of 4 wings around a central rotunda. The builder sets each unit’s local origin at its rotunda center for easy placement. The rotunda is one-story, octagonal in shape, serving as the hub connecting the four wings. The only entrance to a housing unit is via the rotunda’s single door and a long approach corridor, which the builder places facing the spine. Inside the rotunda, an officer’s desk is placed at the entry and stairs leading underground (for maintenance tunnels) are positioned at the back. Each wing extends outward from the rotunda in an X pattern, with four levels of cells per wing. The builder’s algorithm uses parametric dimensions from canon: e.g. corridor width ~12 ft, each wing length ~300 ft, with cells of 10×8 ft arranged on either side of a two-tier corridor. It computes positions for every cell in a grid – for instance, ~28 cells per side per wing per floor (yielding up to ~224 cells per wing, or ~896 cells in a 4-floor unit) by default. These numbers can be tuned, and the system supports designating certain wing segments as common areas (e.g. dayrooms or segregated units) instead of cells if needed. The builder ensures that all four wings connect correctly to the rotunda (e.g. aligning doorway coordinates at cardinal directions), producing a seamless X-shaped cellblock. All housing units are placed in a grid-like fashion on the west side, spaced out per design (e.g. 10 units spread out with yards in between).
Recreation Yard and Specialized Facilities: The open areas between and around housing units – such as the main yard and recreation zones – are also generated. The builder can designate a large Yard zone on the west side of the spine, equipped with Yard features (basketball courts, weight piles, bleachers, etc.). A BP_YardFeature blueprint is used for these elements. Coordinates for yard features are relative to the yard’s origin, and the builder connects them with spline-defined walking paths (e.g. 10 ft wide paths linking yard stations). Similarly, other facilities like the Gymnasium (containing the UFC-style fight cage) and the Library can be instantiated as modules adjacent to the housing or yard areas. The gym might be placed near the yard for easy inmate access, and sized according to the specifications (e.g. containing a 30 ft octagonal fight cage and bleachers). The library or educational center can be placed along the spine or connected to a housing unit as needed. Each such location is built using modular pieces but placed according to the narrative layout (for example, gym on one side of the yard, chapel on the east side near admin, etc.).
Basements, Tunnels, and Vertical Alignment: The builder also accounts for vertical layering. Ground level (Floor 1) is set as Z = 0 for both engines. Additional floors (housing unit levels 2–4) are stacked with Z offsets (e.g. each story 12 ft high, so Z = 12 ft, 24 ft, etc. per floor). Beneath ground, a basement level is generated for areas that require it: e.g. under each rotunda, under the chapel, and connecting to maintenance tunnels. The chapel in particular is placed usually on the east side of the prison (within or near the spine’s facilities), and the builder ensures a baptismal chamber with a hidden tunnel entrance beneath it. These subterranean constructions are part of the Escape Systems (detailed later) but the layout generator will carve out space for them (e.g. create a tunnel network layer below Z=0). All geometry (walls, floors, tunnels) is tagged appropriately for navmesh and collision in both engines.
Implementation (Cross-Engine): The Layout System is implemented as a set of reusable prefabs (Unity) and Blueprint actors (Unreal) that can be programmatically instantiated. In Unreal Engine 5, one could create an Editor Utility or Python script that calls engine APIs to spawn these modules at the right coordinates (e.g. using unreal.EditorLevelLibrary.spawn_actor_from_class for Blueprints and then adjusting their transforms). In Unity, a custom editor script or a manager PrisonBuilder MonoBehaviour can procedurally instantiate Prefabs for each module (using Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation)). The system uses a data-driven approach: a configuration file (JSON or ScriptableObject) can list how many of each module and their relative locations, so the builder can loop through and construct accordingly. By using consistent units and coordinate systems (1 unit = 1 foot in both engines) the same config can drive both Unity and UE5 builds. The result is a fully modular prison layout that matches Nyghtshade Hollow’s canonical design, while allowing easy modifications (e.g. scaling number of cellblocks or resizing wings) thanks to parameterized modules and generation scripts. All structural elements are labeled and organized hierarchically (e.g. grouped under parent empties like “HousingUnits” or “Perimeter”) to keep the scene orderly and extensible.
Factions & Zone Control System
The Factions & Zone Control system overlays gameplay logic onto the physical layout, dividing the prison into zones and tracking which group controls each area. Nyghtshade Hollow’s narrative features complex social dynamics – rival inmate gangs, a powerful inmate boss in the yard, guard factions, etc. – and the builder integrates these by marking zones and linking them to faction data. This ensures the physical map isn’t just static geometry, but a living territory map that can shift as the simulation runs. Key aspects include:
Zone Definitions: The builder breaks the map into named zones or sectors – e.g. Housing Unit A (wing 1), Mess Hall, The Yard, Gym, Library, Chapel, Barrio (Commissary), Admin Wing, Visitation, etc. Each zone is defined by spatial boundaries (which can be volumes or groups of tiles). For instance, each cellblock wing or each distinct facility room is a zone. Zones can also be larger combined areas like an entire housing unit comprising multiple wings. The system assigns each zone a unique ID and type (e.g. “Residential/Cellblock”, “Recreation”, “Workshop”, “Secure/Admin”). These zones are the units of territory control.
Faction Ownership & Influence: Each zone has a property for which faction currently controls or influences it. Factions in Nyghtshade Hollow include inmate groups (gangs, lifers, “new fish” newbies, etc.) and staff groups (guards, administrators). For example, the builder might initialize the main Yard zone as controlled by the “Alpha Inmates” faction (perhaps led by Maddox “X” Thatcher, the inmate who “runs the yard”), while the Barrio commissary could be neutral or contested territory, and the Admin zones controlled by the Warden/guards. Faction data is defined in a config (with unique faction IDs and names). At runtime, the Zone Control system can update these assignments dynamically – e.g. if a riot allows a gang to take over the library, the zone’s controllingFaction field is updated to the new owner. This mapping allows game logic to query “who controls this area” at any time, influencing NPC behavior and player interactions.
Security Level and Access Rules: In addition to faction, each zone has a security level setting and related access rules. Security level (e.g. Minimum, Medium, Max, Solitary) dictates who is allowed in or what precautions exist. The builder can tag zones like Admin or certain housing wings as high-security, requiring special keys or clearance to enter, whereas zones like the Yard or cafeteria are general population areas. These settings interface with the AI and gameplay logic: guards might challenge or attack inmates found in unauthorized zones, and certain faction activities only occur in low-security areas out of staff sight. The Warden’s office and sensitive areas in the Spine would be max security by default. The Zone Control system includes triggers like lockdown states: a lockdown (global or per-zone) can override normal rules to temporarily seal doors and mark zones as off-limits to all inmates. (This ties in with Warden’s control logic, see below.) Each zone blueprint could have an array of door actors or entry points that respond to a lockdown flag (closed for inmates, maybe even for guards depending on scenario).
Smuggling Routes & Contraband Control: Zones are also annotated with contraband risk and smuggling routes, linking into both Faction and Escape systems. For instance, a supply closet or kitchen zone might be marked as a contraband spawn point (where smuggling is easier), and factions that control those zones gain access to more illicit goods. The builder can define hidden connections between zones for smuggling: e.g. a ventilation duct linking the workshop to a cell block, or the classic laundry cart route to move items. These are represented in data as edges between zones that only certain factions/NPCs know about. Factions can thus have influence networks – if they control both ends of a smuggling route, that route is “open” for business. The Zone Control system will keep track of active smuggling corridors, perhaps as part of the tunnel graph or as separate links. This ties into gameplay by affecting contraband availability and triggering events (e.g. a busted smuggling tunnel could spark a crackdown).
Persistent and Dynamic Territory: The design supports dynamic changes in zone control. As the game runs, territory can shift due to events like gang fights or guard crackdowns. The system should log these changes (possibly to the persistent save system), so that across game sessions the faction territories evolve (matching the idea of a “persistent prison ecosystem” with faction wars and hierarchies). Each zone’s last known controlling faction and status can be saved so that if the simulation spans multiple sessions, the world state resumes correctly. Tools are provided to visualize the current faction map (see Visual Hierarchy section) and easily adjust for testing (e.g. a debug command to “swap control of Zone X to Faction Y”).
Implementation Details: We implement a ZoneManager class (or UE5 subsystem) to initialize and manage zones. Each zone can be represented by a Zone data structure:
// Pseudocode (language-agnostic)
class Zone {
    string id;
    string name;
    ZoneType type;
    Faction controllingFaction;
    SecurityLevel securityLevel;
    bool lockdown;  // whether zone is currently locked down
    List<Zone*> connectedZones;  // for adjacency or smuggling links
    List<EntryPoint> entrances;  // doors/gates leading into the zone
}
In Unreal, zones might correspond to Volume actors or tagged level streaming sublevels. In Unity, zones could be empty GameObjects with colliders marking their area or a script that holds references to child objects. The ZoneManager loads initial zone configurations (perhaps from a JSON defining each zone and initial faction owner). It also listens to game events: e.g., if a riot event outcome says “faction A takes over zone B”, the manager updates the controllingFaction for that zone and fires an event (which AI and UI can listen to, updating NPC routines or the map display). Security level changes (like raising a zone to lockdown) are similarly handled via functions in ZoneManager that toggle door locks and signal AI to adjust behavior (guards swarm, inmates retreat to cells, etc.). We also define a Faction class/struct (with fields like name, type (inmate or staff), resources, etc.) and maintain a registry of factions. Factions may have global attributes (like relationships with each other) influencing if they will contest a zone or not. This subsystem is built to be engine-neutral: we keep the logic in plain C++ (for Unreal) or C# (for Unity) without engine-specific calls, while using engine hooks for the spatial queries (like checking if a character is in a zone via collision triggers). By integrating the Factions & Zone Control layer, the Prison Builder ensures that every physical space in Nyghtshade Hollow has meaning in the narrative power structure. For example, if the chapel zone is controlled by a certain religious gang, that will reflect in NPC dialogue and events there. If the workshop is under guard control, players might need a disguise or inside help to access it. This system upholds the canon that factions vie for influence and territory throughout the prison, turning the static map into a dynamic risk/reward landscape for gameplay.
Interaction Points & Event Triggers
To bring the prison to life, the builder sets up Interaction Points – specific locations or objects in the environment where gameplay interactions occur – and ties them into event scripting. These include places where players can perform actions (e.g. initiating an escape attempt, trading contraband, triggering a riot) as well as passive environmental storytelling elements (e.g. overhearing gossip at the yard bleachers). The module defines these points during the construction phase so that they align perfectly with the layout and narrative logic. Major interaction areas and their implementation are as follows:
The Octagon (Gym Fight Arena): The gym contains a regulation-size UFC-style Octagon cage for inmate fights, a central piece of prison culture and one of the core “interactive” setpieces. The builder will place a specialized actor BP_FightArena at the gym’s center to represent this cage. This actor has components for managing fight events: trigger volumes for entering the ring, scoreboards or cameras for streaming fights (as diegetic screens on the cell block TVs, for example), and tie-ins to the stat system. When a player or NPC enters the cage, an event trigger can initiate a fight sequence (governed by combat AI). The Octagon actor is linked to the gymnasium zone’s faction control – whichever faction dominates the gym might influence the fight rules or earn betting profits. The builder also adds spectator interaction points: e.g. marking spots on an upper mezzanine or around the cage where inmates gather to watch (with a "SpectatorPoint" tag). NPCs will route to these points during scheduled fight events, creating the crowd. The outcome of fights can trigger events (rewards in the DC digital currency for winners and bettors) and persistent reputation changes. Because the Octagon is such a key gameplay element, the builder ensures it’s flagged as a Safe Interaction Zone during non-fight times – meaning the game might prevent random violence in the ring outside of sanctioned fights (the ring is only “active” during events). This parallels the idea of certain areas being off-limits for fights unless conditions are met (similar to how the chapel is a no-violence safe zone).
The Chapel & Secret Tunnel Access: The prison chapel serves both as a narrative hub (religious services, a place for covert meetings) and a key interaction point for escape. The builder marks the baptismal font area of the chapel with a hidden trigger linked to the tunnel system. This might be a special actor BP_TunnelEntrance that stays disabled or hidden until certain conditions are met (e.g. the player has obtained a tunnel map or a key from an NPC). Using this interaction point initiates an escape mission or side-quest – for example, opening the secret passage under the chapel floor. Additionally, the chapel is flagged as a Safe Zone (no fighting or open criminal activity here, enforced by game logic in line with canon rules). Interaction points in the chapel might include talking to the priest or an NPC during services, or hiding contraband in pews. Events tied to the chapel could be spiritual events (a scheduled mass that players can attend to boost morale or meet certain NPCs) and investigative triggers (e.g. if the Warden suspects the chapel’s secret, a surprise shakedown event can occur here). The builder ensures the chapel’s placement aligns with the tunnel network below (detailed in Escape Systems) so that the “Chapel Access” to tunnels is functional in game.
The Barrio (Commissary) and Economy Interactions: The Barrio is the inmate commissary – a marketplace inside the prison where inmates trade and purchase goods. The builder will create a dedicated zone/building for the commissary (likely near the center or accessible from multiple housing units). Within the Barrio, it places interaction points like shop counters or NPC vendor stalls. For example, a CommissaryVendor NPC spawn point behind a secure window, and several browse shelves or kiosks for inmates. The UI for buying items (snacks, toiletries, even contraband) is tied to these interaction points. We use a BP_ShopTerminal actor or simply an area trigger that opens the commissary menu when the player approaches. The economy logic (using the prison’s DC currency) is integrated: players can spend DC on items, and prices or stock may be influenced by which faction controls the commissary zone. For example, if a gang takes over the Barrio, certain goods (like shanks or phones) might only be available via the black market at higher prices. The builder also adds event triggers for commissary day – e.g. a weekly event where new stock arrives and lines form, which could be an opportunity for conflict or quests (like intercepting a package). Another interaction is job assignments: an NPC in the commissary might offer the player a work detail (maintaining canon that work programs tie into commissary profits and privileges). Completing jobs could reward DC or improve reputation. These interactions make the Barrio not just a static shop but a dynamic social hub with gameplay impact.
Library & Gym Training Areas: The Library is set up as an interaction zone for intellectual progression. The builder can place desks or computer terminals as interaction points where the player can study or access information (mini-games for skill gains, e.g. improve “Psychology” or “Anatomy” knowledge which then ties into gameplay advantages). It might spawn a librarian NPC (possibly the nurse Bridget moonlighting with her art and psychology background) whom the player can talk to for quests or lore. The Gym (outside of the fight cage) also has training interaction points: weight benches, punching bags, a pull-up bar, etc. These allow the player to perform training actions to increase stats (Strength, Stamina, etc.), with diminishing returns per day. The builder will scatter these props in the gym yard area and tag them with scripts for stat increase mini-games (ensuring the stat system is unified with these points). Such points might be limited by faction control or reputation – e.g. certain equipment is “claimed” by a gang and using it might trigger a confrontation unless you have their respect.
Workshops and Other Facilities: Nyghtshade Hollow includes various work program areas (license plate shop, kitchen, laundry) per real prison design. The builder includes these rooms and places Interaction Stations in each that tie to crafting or missions. For example, in the Workshop, a crafting bench interaction could allow players to assemble improvised tools or weapons if they have stolen components. In the Kitchen, the player might take a cooking job (improving a skill or sneaking extra food for favors). These interactions feed into broader systems – e.g. making shivs in the workshop ties into escape or combat, while working kitchen duty could be a cover for smuggling contraband (hiding items in food trays, etc.). Each station will have triggers or NPCs (like a foreman or guard supervising) so that using them can trigger events (like if you craft a weapon, maybe a random search event could occur). The builder’s role is to ensure these objects are placed in the correct locations and tagged appropriately so the game logic knows what each is for.
Scheduled Events & Routine Triggers: Beyond specific objects, the builder also sets up timed event triggers tied to locations: for instance, a morning roll call event in each housing unit (trigger at a set time in the rotunda area, gathering NPCs), mealtime events in the chow hall, night lockdown in cell blocks, etc. These are essentially invisible triggers or markers the AI uses to move NPCs and prompt player objectives. The builder could place an empty GameObject or a marker actor in relevant zones with an attached script that signals the schedule controller. For example, a MorningRollCallTrigger in each housing rotunda that, at 8:00 in-game time, causes an event “RollCall at Unit A” to fire – NPCs go to their cell doors, guards come to count, and the player gets a prompt to be in place or face punishment. Similarly, chapel service every Sunday in the chapel zone, fight tournament every Friday in the Octagon, etc., can be defined. Having these event hooks laid out spatially helps orchestrate the daily life simulation, a core pillar of gameplay.
Implementation: Interaction points are implemented as a combination of trigger volumes (colliders) and scripted actors. In Unreal, one might use Blueprint Actors with OnComponentBeginOverlap events to detect player/NPC presence and then call into a central Event Manager. In Unity, one could use colliders with scripts (MonoBehaviours) that implement OnTriggerEnter and similarly notify a manager or directly initiate UI/interaction logic. To organize them, the Prison Builder might attach these interaction scripts during construction: e.g., after placing the gym blueprint, it finds the cage object and attaches a FightTrigger component to it, and spawns spectator point empties around. We maintain a registry of interaction points, possibly as part of the Zone data (each Zone can list important interaction IDs it contains). This way, the Faction system and event system can reference them (for example, disabling the commissary shop if a zone is locked down by the Warden). Documentation will list each interaction type and its purpose, so designers or modders know what each point does. The codebase includes stub handlers for each (e.g., void OnOctagonEntered(Player p) or Event BakeBread(Player p) in the kitchen) that tie into stat changes, quest triggers, or mini-games. All these interactions are built to reinforce the narrative tone and systems – brutality in the fight club, intellectual growth in the library, covert ops in the chapel, entrepreneurial smuggling in the commissary – fully aligning with Nyghtshade Hollow’s lore of “a place where brutality, intelligence, and ambition collide”.
Escape Systems (Tunnels & Smuggling Routes)
The Escape Systems module handles all content related to escaping the prison, particularly the network of old tunnels under Nyghtshade Hollow and various escape or smuggling routes built into the design. This system overlaps with both the physical builder (creating the geometry for tunnels) and gameplay logic (managing secret routes, tracking discovered vs. undiscovered passages, and handling escape attempts). Maintaining canon integrity is crucial here: the tunnels originated from an old military base and were supposedly sealed, but in truth many remain accessible, with a famous breakout of 33 inmates using them. The builder will implement this as follows:
Tunnel Network Generation: Beneath the prison’s ground level, the builder generates an underground tunnel network that mirrors parts of the above-ground layout. Historically, these tunnels run from the old base infrastructure, so they connect key points: e.g. from under the chapel (the baptismal font access) outward beyond the prison fences, and possibly between various facility basements. The builder can represent the tunnels as a graph of nodes and corridors. One major corridor might run under the central Spine north-south, with branches reaching under each housing unit (connecting to the rotunda stairwells). Another branch goes to the chapel and then to an external exit (perhaps a drainage conduit in the woods outside). The contractor faked the seals decades ago, so the builder marks certain tunnel segments as “sealed” with thin barriers. These sealed sections are breakable or fake – e.g. modeled as a brick wall that can be removed by determined inmates. The generation of tunnels could use a simplified grid or coordinate offset from the main layout to ensure they line up with access points (for example, the chapel tunnel entrance node is placed directly under the chapel actor’s coordinates). We ensure at least one viable path from inside to outside exists (initially hidden), to allow the canonical mass escape scenario. The geometry for tunnels includes narrow corridors, maintenance rooms, and maybe old storage or utility chambers, reflecting 1930s-40s construction. The builder might reuse scaled-down corridor pieces for this or create unique tunnel segments (with low ceilings, brick-and-concrete textures, etc.). All tunnels are placed on a sub-level with proper collision and navmesh, but initially flagged as unknown/blocked in game logic.
Escape Route Mapping & Data: Each distinct route (a path from a starting zone to an exit) is stored in data so the game can manage it. For instance, a route might be defined as: “Chapel font -> Main Tunnel -> North Drain -> Outside fence”. We define these routes in a JSON or scriptable object list, with properties like isDiscovered (by the player or factions), difficulty, required tools, and triggers when used. The builder’s role is to instantiate any physical markers for these routes: e.g., spawn a loose grate or a diggable patch of ground at the outside exit. We can attach interactive components to these (like a DigExitTrigger on a patch that when used with a shovel leads out). Internally, an EscapeManager system uses the route definitions to check if conditions are met to attempt escape (all required zones must be accessible, tools acquired, etc.). The tunnels and escape routes can also double as smuggling routes when used in smaller scope – e.g. sneaking contraband in rather than a full escape. The data will not differentiate in structure; it’s more about scale (a smuggling route might go from the loading dock to a cell block, entirely within prison bounds, whereas an escape route goes from inside to outside).
Dynamic Events and Challenges: The Escape System isn’t just static geometry – it manages the gameplay challenges of using those routes. The builder helps by placing relevant event triggers in the tunnels: for example, a motion sensor or old alarm halfway through a tunnel that might still be active, represented by a trigger volume that can initiate an alarm event (if the player hasn’t disabled power in an earlier quest). Or collapsed sections that require excavation (we can place a destructible wall actor tagged as “CollapseObstacle”). Some tunnels might contain hazards – e.g. gas pipes (poisonous air) or rodents – to be handled in gameplay. The builder positions these hazards according to narrative (perhaps the southern tunnel is partially flooded, so we mark that segment as requiring a raft or swimming skill). The tension of unknown access points is also represented: the builder may create a few tunnel segments that don’t immediately connect anywhere in the current layout – essentially mystery tunnels that end in sealed walls under the prison. These could later be revealed as leading to new areas or just serve as red herrings that fuel inmate rumors (e.g. “there’s said to be a tunnel under the old laundry that leads to the river”).
Integration with Prison State (Lockdowns & Pursuits): The Escape System tightly integrates with the prison’s security response. If an escape attempt is detected or fails partway, it should trigger consequences. The builder ensures that each tunnel exit or critical point has an attached alarm trigger linked to the prison’s security system. For example, breaching the outer fence line via a tunnel triggers a siren and changes the global state to Lockdown. In Lockdown, the Zone Control system marks all inmate zones as locked, spawns additional guards (perhaps the builder pre-places extra guard spawn points at strategic locations for such scenarios), and possibly toggles off some interaction points (no commissary, no yard time during lockdown). This dynamic was specified in the design: failed escapes lead to increased lockdown levels, altered staff patterns, and punitive transfers. So, the code will include hooks like EscapeManager.OnEscapeAttemptFailed that calls functions in ZoneManager and AIManager to enact these changes (e.g., ZoneManager.SetLockdown(true) for all zones, spawn emergency response guards, etc.). If an escape attempt succeeds (player reaches an outside node unseen), the game might transition to an end state or next chapter (outside world scenario), but in simulation terms, it would remove that inmate from the prison population and record the success. The builder’s data helps here by clearly delineating the path taken and whether it was known to NPCs (e.g. if the path was discovered, guards might already be patrolling it, making escape harder).
Contraband and Backflow: Tunnels aren’t only for escaping people – they’re also pipelines for contraband into the prison. The Escape System overlaps with the economy: certain tunnel routes might be used by corrupt staff or outside accomplices to smuggle drugs, phones, or even weapons inside. The builder can include a drop point in a tunnel (like a loose brick or a dead drop container) that corresponds to a quest or dynamic event (an inmate faction awaiting a package delivery through the tunnel). The data can treat these similarly to escape routes, but flagged as one-way inbound smuggling. NPC AI for factions will utilize these if they control the necessary zones. For example, if a gang controls the chapel, they effectively control its tunnel entrance and thus have a steady contraband supply line (reflected in the economy by that faction having more contraband items available). The system will need to periodically simulate such smuggling runs; the builder’s role is making sure each route has defined start/end points and possible intercept points (where players or guards could catch smugglers).
Implementation: The tunnels themselves are constructed as part of level geometry. In UE5, we might use a combination of pre-modeled tunnel pieces and procedural spline meshes to fit between key points. The builder script can take two anchor transforms (e.g. chapel basement and a point outside fence) and generate a tunnel mesh connecting them, adding midpoint nodes if needed. In Unity, similar approach with prefabs for straight or curved tunnel pieces assembled between waypoints. All tunnels are placed on a separate layer or scene for clarity. For tracking and logic, we create an EscapeRoute data model:
{
  "id": "ChapelEscapeRoute",
  "pathNodes": ["Chapel_Basement", "MainTunnel_Junction", "NorthPerimeterDrain"],
  "requires": ["ShovelTool", "FactionHelp"], 
  "discoveredByPlayer": false,
  "guardPatrol": false
}
This example indicates a route from the chapel basement to a perimeter drain outside. It requires a shovel and some faction’s help to use, and currently guards are not patrolling it (guardPatrol=false). The EscapeManager in code will load such definitions and coordinate with AI: if guardPatrol becomes true (e.g. Warden learns of the tunnel), it will inform the AI system to send guard NPCs to those tunnel nodes periodically. The manager also monitors if the player or any NPC enters a tunnel zone – possibly via trigger volumes – and then executes the appropriate logic (e.g., start an “Escape minigame” or stealth sequence). We also integrate an “Urban Legend” aspect: not all tunnels are known to the player or even the NPCs. Some data entries might exist but discoveredByPlayer false and also unknown to factions until certain clues are found. This means the game can later reveal new escape possibilities as the story progresses (keeping the sense of mystery alive, as per canon inmate rumors about tunnels). The Escape Systems implementation emphasizes extensibility – designers can add new routes by defining their nodes and requirements without altering core code. It remains compatible with both engines: the route logic is platform-agnostic, and only the generation of meshes or the handling of triggers differ slightly (Unreal might use Blueprint for the alarm trigger vs. Unity using C# events, for instance). Ultimately, this module ensures the prison builder produces not just a prison to be contained in, but a playground for escape gameplay, honoring the story of large-scale breakouts and hidden passages that “turn the prison into a living, breathing, persistent ecosystem” of schemes and desperation.
Visual Hierarchy & Admin/Player View Modes
To maintain both gameplay fairness and provide useful tools for developers/administrators, the Prison Builder includes features for different visual and informational perspectives between an admin (or debugging) view and the normal player view. This “Visual Hierarchy” toolset ensures that certain data (like zone ownership, contraband routes, NPC AI nodes) can be visualized from a top-down or omniscient perspective without exposing them in the regular gameplay view, preserving immersion and challenge. Key components of this system:
Admin Overlay Map: The builder can generate an overview map of the prison, essentially a schematic that highlights zones, important points, and possibly real-time status. In Unreal, this could be achieved with a 2D renderer or an orthographic camera above the level that is only activated in Admin mode. In Unity, a separate scene or an overlay UI can be drawn. The map uses color-coding and icons to denote important info: for example, coloring zones by faction control (e.g. red tint for zones under gang control, blue for guard control), marking locations of active events (riots, fights) with symbols, and drawing lines for known tunnel routes. The builder, having all zone and faction data, feeds this map generation. If running in a development environment, the map can be updated live; if used as a gameplay feature (say the player character is the Warden with access to security monitors), it can be toggled via an in-game interface. This overhead “blueprint view” of the prison aids in debugging the simulation and also plays into the narrative of a high-tech security system at the Warden’s disposal.
Perspective-Based Detail Filtering: We implement rules such that certain objects or indicators only appear in certain views. For instance, hidden tunnels and contraband stashes are invisible in normal player view (unless the player has discovered them via gameplay), but in Admin/Dev mode these could be rendered with debug materials or gizmos. Similarly, NPC patrol routes or navigation nodes can be visualized in the editor or admin mode as splines or waypoints, which is useful for level designers to verify AI path networks. The builder can automatically include gizmo components on key actors (like an arrow path for each guard’s patrol route, or a sphere marker at each interaction point) that are set to EditorOnly (Unreal) or Debug layers (Unity). This way, they won’t show up in the shipped game, but a developer can load the project and see a full annotation of the level. If an in-game admin mode is planned (for a potential “Warden mode” gameplay), these could be toggled via UI to simulate what a high-level security system would display (for example, turning on a heatmap of recent fights or camera feeds).
Security Camera System: The prison is likely covered by CCTV cameras. The builder places security camera actors at strategic points (corners of corridors, overlooking yards, inside common areas). Each camera is an object with a frustum and can render to a render-texture or be used as a viewpoint. In admin mode (or Warden gameplay), the user can cycle through these camera feeds. Implementing this means both engines need camera switching logic: in UE5, we could use SceneCapture2D for live feeds or simply possess different cameras; in Unity, use multiple Camera objects and render to quads or use a Picture-in-Picture. The builder, having a list of recommended camera locations (covering all major zones), will spawn them and maybe assign IDs (like “Cam 1 – A Block Hallway”). In debug mode, we might also draw each camera’s coverage as a colored cone or outline in the scene view to ensure there are no blind spots. This ties into the Visual Hierarchy because it’s a layer of information the Warden/AI has that players (in inmate role) do not – unless they tap into it by hacking cameras, which could be a gameplay element.
In-Game Admin Console / Dashboard: The plan calls for cross-engine compatibility and even external monitoring tools. We envision a web or in-game dashboard (possibly built with React/TypeScript for a web UI, as some design notes indicated) that can display prison stats: faction influence levels, inmate morale, active events, etc. The builder module can include a component that collects all game state info (zones, factions, NPC info) and exposes it (maybe via an API or debug menu). This could be as simple as writing out a JSON snapshot of the world or as involved as a live link to a web interface. For example, an external dashboard might show a list of all factions with current territory and an emoji icon summary (per earlier style guidelines, using emojis to indicate different categories for clarity). Or it might list all ongoing events (🔴 riot in Yard, 🟢 routine rollcall in Unit B, etc.). While this goes slightly beyond the in-engine “builder” itself, it is a complementary tool that was mentioned in the context of fully monitoring the simulation. The builder ensures that all necessary data hooks (like events broadcasting updates) are in place so such a dashboard is feasible. In Unreal or Unity, this might be achieved with a simple HTTP server running or by writing logs that an external program reads.
Developer Tools Integration: For level designers, the module provides convenience tools. This includes navmesh generation toggles (after building the layout, automatically build or update navmesh in editor – indeed the process can call Unreal’s EditorLevelLibrary.build_navigation() as seen in the logs). Also, an AI navgrid builder is integrated, which can automatically place Navigation modifiers or waypoints in critical areas (for example, marking rotunda areas as preferred path hubs for AI). Additionally, hooks like a lighting rig deployer (auto-placing template light actors in each area with correct settings for mood) and a pathfinding anchor generator (points that help connect internal/external navigation like ladders or door links) are part of the builder’s finalization step. These tools operate behind the scenes in editor mode to save developers time – for instance, as soon as a housing unit is spawned, the builder script could drop a predefined set of lights, cameras, and path nodes in it. All such helpers are either non-runtime (editor-only) or conditionally compiled out for shipping builds. They contribute to maintaining a clear visual hierarchy in development: what the dev sees (fully annotated world) versus what the player sees (immersive world with hidden mechanics). Documentation will include a guide for using the Builder’s debug mode, explaining how to toggle these visual layers on/off and interpret them.
Implementation: Implementing the dual-view mode involves conditional rendering and debugging flags. In both engines, we’ll have a global boolean (or a mode enum) for DebugMode or AdminView. Many actor classes in the builder (Zone, Camera, InteractionPoint) will check this flag in their BeginPlay or Editor construction script to decide whether to spawn debug visuals. For example, a Zone volume might, in editor, draw a colored transparent box with the zone’s name and controlling faction label floating above it, but mark those debug meshes to not appear in game. Unreal’s Development only conditional compilation or WITH_EDITOR checks can be used in C++ code; Unity can use #if UNITY_EDITOR or runtime checks for a debug key press. The security camera feeds feature requires some UI work: in Unreal, we might leverage UMG to create a surveillance monitor widget that can switch texture feeds. In Unity, an in-game UI canvas with render textures can simulate a CCTV monitor wall. The React/TypeScript dashboard would be an external tool – we could generate a JSON file of all relevant data each frame or at intervals, and use a Node.js/Express app to serve a webpage that visualizes it (this is outside the game runtime, but the pieces in-game ensure the data is available). All these are considered part of the Prison Builder toolkit as they emerge from the initial generation process (the builder doesn’t just place walls; it also seeds the level with all these monitoring points and debug hooks). By providing a clear separation of player view vs. admin/dev view, the module supports both the game’s realism (players can’t magically see through walls or know who controls what without in-world clues) and the developer’s oversight (easy debugging of AI and systems). This dual approach aligns with the idea that Nyghtshade Hollow is not only a game world but also a complex simulation that needs oversight – much like a real prison has its control room for guards versus the limited perspective of inmates. We thus ensure readability (clear visual cues in editor), extensibility (new debug overlays can be added as new systems come in), and canon integrity (the player experience remains diegetic – e.g., if the player gains an “admin view”, it’s because they earned it in the narrative, say by accessing the Warden’s security system, not because the game just exposed raw data).
Engine Compatibility and Integration Notes
The Prison Builder module is designed to be engine-agnostic at its core, with specific integration layers for Unreal Engine 5 and Unity. This ensures that all features above – layout generation, faction control logic, interactions, escape systems, and debug tools – work in either engine with minimal changes, fulfilling the cross-engine requirement. Below is an outline of how the codebase is structured for each engine and what considerations were taken for compatibility:
Core Data and Logic Layer: We separate the game logic into a core module (which could be a library or just a conceptual separation) that doesn’t depend on engine-specific API. This includes data structures for zones, factions, escape routes, etc., and logic for updating game state. For instance, determining faction takeover of a zone or calculating an escape route’s requirements can be done in plain C# or C++ code without assuming anything about Unity or Unreal. We maintain this in parallel for both languages: a set of C# scripts in Unity (maybe inside an Assembly Definition for clarity) and a set of C++ classes (or even Blueprint-friendly C++ classes) in Unreal. By keeping algorithms and data pure, we ensure consistency across engines – the same input conditions produce the same outcomes. Unit tests (where possible) can be written to validate logic in isolation.
Engine-Specific Builders: The actual construction of the scene/level is where engine specifics come in. We implement a PrisonBuilderSystem in each engine:
In Unreal Engine 5, we can create an Editor Utility Widget or Blueprint Editor script that reads a high-level layout config and spawns the appropriate BP_ actors. We might also use the Python API for Unreal (as some steps in the conversation logs suggest) to automate tasks like building nav meshes and saving levels. The builder could be packaged as an Editor Plugin for UE5, providing a button like “Generate Nyghtshade Hollow” which when clicked executes the generation script. All Blueprint classes (BP_HousingUnit, BP_SpineSegment, etc.) are organized in folders (for example, Content/PrisonBuilder/Blueprints/) and the plugin ensures they are loaded. We have taken care to align units and measurements with real-world scale for UE (using 1uu = 1 foot, instead of the default 1uu = 1cm, which might involve scaling our world accordingly). If needed, we adjust the World Settings in UE to use a convenient scale, or simply handle conversion in our builder code (multiply positions by 0.3048 if we treat 1uu as 1cm internally).
In Unity, the builder can be implemented as an EditorWindow script (in C#). For example, a custom menu item “Nyghtshade Hollow -> Generate Prison” that opens a configuration GUI. When run, it programmatically creates GameObjects for each module (using PrefabUtility.InstantiatePrefab in the editor context, or regular instantiation if run at play mode). Prefabs corresponding to each piece (walls, cell blocks, etc.) are stored in a Unity folder (Assets/PrisonBuilder/Prefabs). We again use 1 unit = 1 foot for consistency, meaning if the data says “300 ft tunnel”, we position the end object at 300 units away. Unity’s NavMesh components can be baked at runtime or via the editor after generation (we can call NavMesh.Surface.Bake() if using the NavMeshSurface system). Lighting in Unity might need adjusting since our scale is large – we include recommended light probe placement or use runtime GI if needed.
Synchronizing Content: Some assets (models, textures) are shared between engines (via FBX, PNG, etc.). For example, the wall and floor materials (black walls with crimson stripes) are a key aesthetic. We ensure the stripe textures and materials are provided for both: in UE, perhaps a Material Instance with parameters for stripe width; in Unity, a ShaderGraph or material with a similar setup. The builder’s code might procedurally apply these materials – e.g., after creating walls, assign the “BlackConcreteWithRedStripes” material to them. To keep parity, we maintain an Asset Manifest that lists assets and their engine-specific references (like in UE it might be /Game/PrisonBuilder/Materials/M_WallStripe and in Unity Materials/WallStripe.mat). The builder looks up the appropriate one depending on the engine. All special interactive objects (like the fight cage, security cameras, etc.) also have equivalents in both engines, either as exported models or created procedurally (the cage could be generated via code as an 8-sided polygon fence, or simply be a pre-made mesh).
Differences and Engine Strengths: While the core design is the same, we leverage each engine’s strengths. In Unreal, Blueprints and the Behavior Tree system can be used for the AI of guards and inmates with faction awareness. In Unity, we might rely on a more custom C# AI solution or integrate a package. The builder abstracts these: for instance, it will place AI spawn points and waypoints (in Unreal, maybe using Target Points or a custom APatrolNode actor; in Unity, empty GameObjects with a script). The actual AI logic is beyond the builder’s immediate scope but needs those anchors. We add engine-specific notes in documentation: e.g., “In Unreal, assign the PatrolNode class to these points and link to AI Controller; in Unity, ensure NavMeshAgent and a Patrol script use these points list.” Cross-engine notes are provided as inline comments or separate sections. Another difference is lighting and performance: UE5 can handle large scenes with its World Partition or level streaming – we can split the prison into sublevels by wings to use that. In Unity, we might need to bake occlusion culling or use sections selectively active. The builder includes options for that (like a toggle to mark all objects in a housing unit as static for occlusion, or to create sections as additive scenes).
Testing and Validation: After generation, we run validation steps in each engine. For UE5, the builder can log a message (“Nyghtshade Hollow build complete”) and even save out the level file. It can also run the navmesh build as seen in the script and any other compile steps. For Unity, we might run an Editor test to ensure every expected object exists (e.g. exactly N cells per wing, etc.). We can include Gizmo drawing in Unity to replicate the helpful debug visuals from Unreal. Both engines will have a Play Mode test where we spawn a dummy player character and ensure they can walk through a door, go from a cell to yard, etc., using the navmesh to confirm connectivity. These steps are documented so a developer following the plan knows how to verify the builder’s output quickly.
In summary, the codebase is organized such that common game logic is mirrored in both C++ (UE) and C# (Unity) implementations, with careful attention to using the same parameters and formulas (for sizes, counts, etc.) so the worlds match in scale and content. Where engine-specific features are used, we isolate them: for example, a separate file for “UnityPrisonBuilder.cs” and “UEPrisonBuilder.cpp” each handling the spawning and engine API calls, but both relying on shared data definitions from a higher-level design (like a JSON blueprint of the prison). The documentation includes a Cross-Engine Implementation Guide explaining how each major system is realized in Unreal vs Unity, ensuring developers can achieve feature parity. This approach guarantees that Nyghtshade Hollow’s prison can exist faithfully whether in Unreal’s high-fidelity environment or Unity’s flexible toolkit, and any narrative or rule changes (canon updates) can be propagated by adjusting one set of parameters in the shared config. By prioritizing consistency and clarity, we’ve made the builder’s output predictable and maintainable across platforms.
Security & Warden Control Logic
(Integrating Warden Valentino’s oversight mechanics and prison-wide security systems) A final critical system to discuss is the Security & Warden Control layer, which acts as the top-level governor of the prison. This ties together many of the above systems (factions, zones, escape, events) and provides the means by which a central authority (the Warden AI or player as Warden) can intervene. The builder sets up the scaffolding for these controls so that they align with canonical behaviors – for example, Warden Valentino (“Valley”) is known to exercise tight control, capable of locking inmates out of privileges on a whim. Here’s how the implementation addresses this:
Global Security Manager: We introduce a singleton-like manager (perhaps PrisonSecurityManager) that has oversight of alarms, lockdown states, and system-wide effects. The builder initializes this manager with references to all critical subsystems (ZoneManager, FactionManager, EscapeManager, etc.). When certain high-level events occur (escape attempt, riot, contraband found), this manager executes the appropriate response according to rules. For example, if an inmate is caught in a tunnel, the SecurityManager triggers a Lockdown: it calls ZoneManager to set all zones’ lockdown flag true, calls AI systems to deploy riot squads, and perhaps invokes the UI to broadcast a prison-wide alarm message. The rules for responses can be data-driven (a scriptable “policy” for the Warden), which can be tweaked for difficulty or narrative. The builder doesn’t implement all AI responses itself but provides the hooks and default reactions drawn from the story. E.g., “Failure can increase lockdown levels” is explicitly implemented: each failed escape increments a counter, and the SecurityManager might upgrade the prison’s security level (more frequent searches, etc.).
Warden’s Overrides: In the Nyghtshade Hollow lore, the Warden can directly influence inmate life – e.g. lock someone out of the commissary (freezing their DC account) or reassign them to solitary. The design accounts for this by allowing the SecurityManager (as a proxy for Warden) to send commands to specific systems. We implement functions like RevokeCommissaryAccess(Inmate inmate) or FreezeAccount(inmate) which the game can call when, say, the player upsets the Warden in the story. Under the hood, this might set a flag on that inmate’s profile that the Commissary UI checks and refuses service if true. Or it might temporarily mark the inmate’s faction as “out of privileges” meaning any zone they enter that normally grants something (like library study or gym equipment) will not work for them. Similarly, LockdownZone(zoneId) would bolt a specific area – for instance, if contraband is found in Unit C, Warden might only lock Unit C. The builder ensures every zone and subsystem listens for these overrides. Doors placed by the builder are all wired to a central control system: e.g., each door actor might have a boolean “isLocked” that by default is controlled by schedules, but SecurityManager can flip all to locked. We can achieve this easily by grouping door objects or giving them tags like “LockdownAffected” and having the SecurityManager find all such objects on command.
Canon Safety Measures: The prison builder also installs the physical representations of security measures. For example, manual lockdown controls – perhaps the Warden’s office has a lever or a computer panel that triggers lockdown. We could place an interactable panel object in the Warden’s Tower that is linked to the SecurityManager’s functions (for an in-game representation if the player ever gets access, or if a cutscene needs to show Warden hitting the alarm). We also scatter alarm lights and sirens around the complex (red spinning lights in corridors, loudspeakers) which the builder tags and groups so they can all be activated during emergencies. Testing ensures that when lockdown triggers, these effects play (e.g. in UE, activate a Niagara VFX for alarm lights and a SoundCue for siren). Another measure: surveillance and informant system – though more abstract, it could be represented by placing hidden “microphone” actors in certain spots (maybe not physically visible, but conceptually present). This ties into how the game might detect if the player plans an escape: talking about it in certain areas could raise suspicion if those areas are “bugged.” The builder could mark the chapel confessional or phones in visitation as tapped lines that feed into a probability of Warden learning plans. While this is a deep mechanic, the groundwork is simply identifying those assets/areas.
Balancing and Tunability: All Warden control logic is made tunable via data files or editor settings. Since this is a simulation-heavy game, designers may want to adjust how harsh or reactive the Warden is. The codebase might have a config like: WardenReactionConfig with values like RiotThreshold, SearchFrequency, etc. Warden Valentino’s “management style” in canon could be interpreted into these numbers – e.g., if he’s particularly ruthless, then even small infractions trigger big responses. The builder’s job is to load these settings and ensure all subsystems honor them. For example, if SearchFrequency is high, the builder could schedule additional cell shakedown events (perhaps by adding extra event triggers in the housing units for surprise inspections). If RiotThreshold (how much inmate unrest triggers a lockdown) is low, then the Faction system might automatically call a lockdown if a fight breaks out involving more than X inmates. Documentation will include recommended settings that align with a challenging but fair simulation, and note how to adjust them for alternative play styles.
Implementation: The SecurityManager (Warden AI) can be implemented as a high-level controller either within the game or as an external “AI Director” module. It will likely run as part of the game loop, checking conditions every few in-game minutes. For efficiency and clarity, we script specific events rather than continuous heavy monitoring. For instance, when an escape route breach occurs, the EscapeManager simply calls SecurityManager.OnEscapeDetected(routeId) which triggers the sequence of responses. We avoid one giant monolith by splitting responsibilities: the Warden logic primarily decides when to escalate, whereas each system (Zones, AI, Economy) knows how to implement the change. This modular approach makes the system extensible – new controls can be added (say later we introduce a “drone surveillance” system, the Warden could deploy a drone via a new function, without altering zone code). In Unreal, some of this can be done via Blueprint (like a Director Blueprint that listens to events and toggles things) or via C++ in the GameMode or a custom Manager object. In Unity, it could be an invisible GameObject with a SecurityManager script that’s initialized at scene start. We will use engine message systems to broadcast orders: e.g., in Unity an event or delegate pattern, in Unreal maybe the Gameplay Event system or direct function calls if references are known. All doors and systems will subscribe to a “LockdownStateChanged” event to simplify communication. By embedding this Security & Warden control logic into the builder’s output, we ensure the game’s narrative theme of a tightly controlled prison is upheld. The Warden’s presence is constantly felt through these systems: privileges can be yanked away, zones can be locked down, and the sense that there’s an intelligence monitoring you is tangible. This adds a layer of strategy for the player (finding ways to disable or evade these controls) and gives the simulation a master coordinator so chaos doesn’t spiral endlessly – it gets reined in, just as a real prison warden would attempt to do. In sum, this final piece ties the environment and gameplay together under the rule of law (or tyranny) represented by Warden Valentino, completing the Prison Builder Module as not just a level generator but an integrated prison simulation framework true to Nyghtshade Hollow’s lore and tone.
Documentation & Next Steps:
The codebase will include comprehensive documentation for each system. Key files and their purposes will be outlined (e.g., ZoneManager.cs/.cpp, PrisonBuilder.unrealplugin, InteractionDefs.json, etc.). A README or design document will summarize the architecture so new developers or modders can quickly understand how the prison is constructed and controlled. We will also provide example usage, like how to add a new wing or how to tweak faction starting conditions. The plan prioritizes clean organization (folders for Layout, Factions, Interactions, Escape, Security in the project) and clear naming conventions for all components, making it easy to navigate. By following this implementation plan, one can generate a fully functional prison level that is readable in editor (thanks to logical grouping and debug visuals), extensible for future content (new zones or gameplay elements can hook in via the defined managers and data configs), and canon-faithful (every detail from the octagonal fences to the secret chapel tunnel to the Warden’s all-seeing eye is represented as described in the Nyghtshade Hollow lore). The resulting Prison Builder module sets a strong foundation for Nyghtshade Hollow to become “a living, breathing, persistent prison ecosystem”, ready to challenge and captivate players.

Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2
In this course from Epic Online Learning, we cover the high-level basics of Unreal Engine 5.2. Learn to create new projects using project templates and add custom or premade assets with the Content Browser. Easily add Actors to levels and modify their properties with the Details panel; gain control of environmental lighting and effects with Lighting Actors; and create Blueprint Actors and use the Blueprint Editor to control them. Finally, learn how to package your projects for playtesting and sharing.

📁 Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2 Overview
📁 Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2 Overview
A new engine version means a new first hour! Follow along with this course to create a small project and learn the high-level basics of Unreal Engine 5.2. Learn how to add assets, create lighting, make Blueprints, and even share your project.

RUNNING TIME
51 minutes

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN 
You'll learn how to:
Create new projects using project Templates. 
Add custom or premade assets to existing projects which can be accessed in the Content Browser. 
Add Actors to levels and modify their properties with the Details panel. 
Add and control environmental lighting and effects in a scene with Lighting Actors. 
Use Blueprint Actors with the Blueprint Editor. 
TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS
Course:
Compatible with Unreal Engine 5.2

Compatible with Unreal Engine 5.2

Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2
Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2
In this course from Epic Online Learning, we cover the high-level basics of Unreal Engine 5.2. Learn to create new projects using project templates and add custom or premade assets with the Content Browser. Easily add Actors to levels and modify their properties with the Details panel; gain control of environmental lighting and effects with Lighting Actors; and create Blueprint Actors and use the Blueprint Editor to control them. Finally, learn how to package your projects for playtesting and sharing.

📁 Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2 Overview
📁 Your First Hour in Unreal Engine 5.2 Overview
A new engine version means a new first hour! Follow along with this course to create a small project and learn the high-level basics of Unreal Engine 5.2. Learn how to add assets, create lighting, make Blueprints, and even share your project.

RUNNING TIME
51 minutes

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN 
You'll learn how to:
Create new projects using project Templates. 
Add custom or premade assets to existing projects which can be accessed in the Content Browser. 
Add Actors to levels and modify their properties with the Details panel. 
Add and control environmental lighting and effects in a scene with Lighting Actors. 
Use Blueprint Actors with the Blueprint Editor.

Getting Started with Python in VS Code
In this tutorial, you will learn how to use Python 3 in Visual Studio Code to create, run, and debug a Python "Roll a dice!" application, work with virtual environments, use packages, and more! By using the Python extension, you turn VS Code into a great, lightweight Python editor.

If you are new to programming, check out the Visual Studio Code for Education - Introduction to Python course. This course offers a comprehensive introduction to Python, featuring structured modules in a ready-to-code browser-based development environment.

To gain a deeper understanding of the Python language, you can explore any of the programming tutorials listed on python.org within the context of VS Code.

For a Data Science focused tutorial with Python, check out our Data Science section.

Prerequisites
To successfully complete this tutorial, you need to first set up your Python development environment. Specifically, this tutorial requires:

Python 3
VS Code
VS Code Python extension (For additional details on installing extensions, see Extension Marketplace)
Install a Python interpreter
Along with the Python extension, you need to install a Python interpreter. Which interpreter you use is dependent on your specific needs, but some guidance is provided below.

Windows
Install Python from python.org. Use the Download Python button that appears first on the page to download the latest version.

Note: If you don't have admin access, an additional option for installing Python on Windows is to use the Microsoft Store. The Microsoft Store provides installs of supported Python versions.

For additional information about using Python on Windows, see Using Python on Windows at Python.org

macOS
The system install of Python on macOS is not supported. Instead, a package management system like Homebrew is recommended. To install Python using Homebrew on macOS use brew install python3 at the Terminal prompt.

Note: On macOS, make sure the location of your VS Code installation is included in your PATH environment variable. See these setup instructions for more information.

Linux
The built-in Python 3 installation on Linux works well, but to install other Python packages you must install pip with get-pip.py.

Other options
Data Science: If your primary purpose for using Python is Data Science, then you might consider a download from Anaconda. Anaconda provides not just a Python interpreter, but many useful libraries and tools for data science.

Windows Subsystem for Linux: If you are working on Windows and want a Linux environment for working with Python, the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) is an option for you. If you choose this option, you'll also want to install the WSL extension. For more information about using WSL with VS Code, see VS Code Remote Development or try the Working in WSL tutorial, which will walk you through setting up WSL, installing Python, and creating a Hello World application running in WSL.

Note: To verify that you've installed Python successfully on your machine, run one of the following commands (depending on your operating system):

Linux/macOS: open a Terminal Window and type the following command:

Bash

python3 --version
Windows: open a command prompt and run the following command:

Bat

py -3 --version
If the installation was successful, the output window should show the version of Python that you installed. Alternatively, you can use the py -0 command in the VS Code integrated terminal to view the versions of python installed on your machine. The default interpreter is identified by an asterisk (*).

Start VS Code in a workspace folder
By starting VS Code in a folder, that folder becomes your "workspace".

Using a command prompt or terminal, create an empty folder called "hello", navigate into it, and open VS Code (code) in that folder (.) by entering the following commands:

Bash

mkdir hello
cd hello
code .
Note: If you're using an Anaconda distribution, be sure to use an Anaconda command prompt.

Alternately, you can create a folder through the operating system UI, then use VS Code's File > Open Folder to open the project folder.

Create a virtual environment
A best practice among Python developers is to use a project-specific virtual environment. Once you activate that environment, any packages you then install are isolated from other environments, including the global interpreter environment, reducing many complications that can arise from conflicting package versions. You can create non-global environments in VS Code using Venv or Anaconda with Python: Create Environment.

Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), start typing the Python: Create Environment command to search, and then select the command.

The command presents a list of environment types, Venv or Conda. For this example, select Venv.

Create Environment dropdown

The command then presents a list of interpreters that can be used for your project. Select the interpreter you installed at the beginning of the tutorial.

Virtual environment interpreter selection

After selecting the interpreter, a notification will show the progress of the environment creation and the environment folder (/.venv) will appear in your workspace.

Create environment status notification

Ensure your new environment is selected by using the Python: Select Interpreter command from the Command Palette.

Select an Interpreter

Note: For additional information about virtual environments, or if you run into an error in the environment creation process, see Environments.

Create a Python source code file
From the File Explorer toolbar, select the New File button on the hello folder:

File Explorer New File

Name the file hello.py, and VS Code will automatically open it in the editor:

File Explorer hello.py

By using the .py file extension, you tell VS Code to interpret this file as a Python program, so that it evaluates the contents with the Python extension and the selected interpreter.

Note: The File Explorer toolbar also allows you to create folders within your workspace to better organize your code. You can use the New folder button to quickly create a folder.

Now that you have a code file in your Workspace, enter the following source code in hello.py:

Python

msg = "Roll a dice!"
print(msg)
When you start typing print, notice how IntelliSense presents auto-completion options.

IntelliSense appearing for Python code

IntelliSense and auto-completions work for standard Python modules as well as other packages you've installed into the environment of the selected Python interpreter. It also provides completions for methods available on object types. For example, because the msg variable contains a string, IntelliSense provides string methods when you type msg.:

IntelliSense appearing for a variable whose type provides methods

Finally, save the file (Ctrl+S). At this point, you're ready to run your first Python file in VS Code.

For full details on editing, formatting, and refactoring, see Editing code. The Python extension also has full support for Linting.

Run Python code
Click the Run Python File play button in the top-right side of the editor.

Using the Run Python File button

The button opens a terminal panel in which your Python interpreter is automatically activated, then runs python3 hello.py (macOS/Linux) or python hello.py (Windows):

Program output in a Python terminal

There are three other ways you can run Python code within VS Code:

Right-click anywhere in the editor window and select Run Python > Run Python File in Terminal (which saves the file automatically):

Run Python File in Terminal command in the Python editor

Select one or more lines, then press Shift+Enter or right-click and select Run Python > Run Selection/Line in Python Terminal. Alternatively, you can activate Smart Send using Shift+Enter without a selection and the Python extension will send the smallest runnable block of code near where your cursor is placed to the terminal. This command is convenient for testing just a part of a file.

Note: If you prefer to send code at the particular line your cursor is placed, you can turn off Smart Send by setting python.REPL.enableREPLSmartSend : "false" in your User settings.

From the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), select the Python: Start Terminal REPL command to open a REPL terminal (notated by >>>) for the currently selected Python interpreter. In the REPL, you can then enter and run lines of code one at a time.

Congrats, you just ran your first Python code in Visual Studio Code!

Configure and run the debugger
Let's now try debugging our Python program. Debugging support is provided by the Python Debugger extension, which is automatically installed with the Python extension. To ensure it has been installed correctly, open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X) and search for @installed python debugger. You should see the Python Debugger extension listed in the results.

Python Debugger extension shown in installed extensions view in VS Code.

Next, set a breakpoint on line 2 of hello.py by placing the cursor on the print call and pressing F9. Alternately, click in the editor's left gutter, next to the line numbers. When you set a breakpoint, a red circle appears in the gutter.

Setting a breakpoint in hello.py

Next, to initialize the debugger, press F5. Since this is your first time debugging this file, a configuration menu will open from the Command Palette allowing you to select the type of debug configuration you would like for the opened file.

List of Python debugger configuration options

Note: VS Code uses JSON files for all of its various configurations; launch.json is the standard name for a file containing debugging configurations.

Select Python File, which is the configuration that runs the current file shown in the editor using the currently selected Python interpreter.

The debugger will start, and then stop at the first line of the file breakpoint. The current line is indicated with a yellow arrow in the left margin. If you examine the Local variables window at this point, you can see that the msg variable appears in the Local pane.

Debugging step 2 - variable defined

A debug toolbar appears along the top with the following commands from left to right: continue (F5), step over (F10), step into (F11), step out (Shift+F11), restart (Ctrl+Shift+F5), and stop (Shift+F5).

Debugging toolbar

The Status Bar also changes color (orange in many themes) to indicate that you're in debug mode. The Python Debug Console also appears automatically in the lower right panel to show the commands being run, along with the program output.

To continue running the program, select the continue command on the debug toolbar (F5). The debugger runs the program to the end.

Tip Debugging information can also be seen by hovering over code, such as variables. In the case of msg, hovering over the variable will display the string Roll a dice! in a box above the variable.

You can also work with variables in the Debug Console (If you don't see it, select Debug Console in the lower right area of VS Code, or select it from the ... menu.) Then try entering the following lines, one by one, at the > prompt at the bottom of the console:

Python

msg
msg.capitalize()
msg.split()
Debugging step 3 - using the debug console

Select the blue Continue button on the toolbar again (or press F5) to run the program to completion. "Roll a dice!" appears in the Python Debug Console if you switch back to it, and VS Code exits debugging mode once the program is complete.

If you restart the debugger, the debugger again stops on the first breakpoint.

To stop running a program before it's complete, use the red square stop button on the debug toolbar (Shift+F5), or use the Run > Stop debugging menu command.

For full details, see Debugging configurations, which includes notes on how to use a specific Python interpreter for debugging.

Tip: Use Logpoints instead of print statements: Developers often litter source code with print statements to quickly inspect variables without necessarily stepping through each line of code in a debugger. In VS Code, you can instead use Logpoints. A Logpoint is like a breakpoint except that it logs a message to the console and doesn't stop the program. For more information, see Logpoints in the main VS Code debugging article.

Install and use packages
Let's build upon the previous example by using packages.

In Python, packages are how you obtain any number of useful code libraries, typically from PyPI, that provide additional functionality to your program. For this example, you use the numpy package to generate a random number.

Return to the Explorer view (the top-most icon on the left side, which shows files), open hello.py, and paste in the following source code:

Python

import numpy as np

msg = "Roll a dice!"
print(msg)

print(np.random.randint(1,9))
Tip: If you enter the above code by hand, you may find that auto-completions change the names after the as keywords when you press Enter at the end of a line. To avoid this, type a space, then Enter.

Next, run the file in the debugger using the "Python: Current file" configuration as described in the last section.

You should see the message, "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'". This message indicates that the required package isn't available in your interpreter. If you're using an Anaconda distribution or have previously installed the numpy package you may not see this message.

To install the numpy package, stop the debugger and use the Command Palette to run Terminal: Create New Terminal (Ctrl+Shift+). This command opens a command prompt for your selected interpreter.

To install the required packages in your virtual environment, enter the following commands as appropriate for your operating system:

Install the packages

Bash

# Don't use with Anaconda distributions because they include matplotlib already.

# macOS
python3 -m pip install numpy

# Windows (may require elevation)
python -m pip install numpy

# Linux (Debian)
apt-get install python3-tk
python3 -m pip install numpy
Now, rerun the program, with or without the debugger, to view the output!

Managing dependencies across environments
When working on Python projects, it’s essential to manage your dependencies effectively. One useful tip is to use the pip freeze > requirements.txt command. This command helps you create a requirements.txt file that lists all the packages installed in your virtual environment. This file can then be used to recreate the same environment elsewhere.

Follow these steps to create a requirements.txt file:

Activate your virtual environment, if you haven’t already.

Bash

source venv/bin/activate  # On macOS/Linux
PowerShell

.\venv\Scripts\activate   # On Windows
Generate the requirements.txt file.

PowerShell

pip freeze > requirements.txt
You can now use the newly generated requirements.txt file to install dependencies in another environment. Furthermore, you can continue to add dependencies to it as your project may grow in complexity.

PowerShell

pip install -r requirements.txt
By following these steps, you ensure that your project dependencies are consistent across different environments, making it easier to collaborate with others and deploy your project.

Congrats on completing the Python tutorial! During the course of this tutorial, you learned how to create a Python project, create a virtual environment, run and debug your Python code, and install Python packages. Explore additional resources to learn how to get the most out of Python in Visual Studio Code!
